#9750. Stripe Pay Turns Stripe Handles Into Free, Instant B2B Transfers

Streamline your payments, simplify your life. Effortless money management, made easy.

Streamline your payments, simplify your life. Effortless money management, made easy.

Streamline your payments, simplify your life. Effortless money management, made easy.

You type a Stripe profile handle. You send. The money lands. No routing numbers, no ACH wait, no wire fee. On October 27, 2026, Stripe introduced "stripe pay" for instant business-to-business transfers, available in the Dashboard and the CLI. The sender needs a funded financial account; the recipient needs one tied to its Stripe profile. Transfers move in USD, GBP or USDC, same currency only, and the product is in preview for eligible US and UK businesses. It is a closed loop inside a network Stripe already runs.

Co-founder Patrick Collison put the thesis plainly: "A2A payments will be more important than P2P payments." Account-to-account beats person-to-person when the volume is vendor invoices, contractor pay and agent settlements. The product is simple because the problem is old. Banks still charge. Banks still delay. Stripe already holds accounts for millions of businesses, and now those accounts can pay each other without the middleman tax.

Vendors get paid the day the work is done instead of next week. Platforms settle with sellers without floating cash. Freelancers abroad can receive USDC faster than a wire. The friction was never the idea of paying another company. It was typing numbers, waiting days and losing points to interchange. Remove those and the use case becomes the default.

Agents are the other audience. The CLI can dry-run a transfer, return machine-readable output, and only send after the user confirms the recipient, amount, currency and funding account. Stripe's own instructions tell agents to look up businesses in Stripe Directory and "don't guess the recipient." That is how an AI agent pays a vendor safely: validate, confirm, then release funds, with a human approving the big ones. HackerNoon has covered the open question underneath all of this: who pays when an AI agent makes the wrong purchase?

Stripe stopped being only a card processor years ago. It added treasury accounts, stablecoins, global payouts and, at Sessions 2026, agent financial accounts that can check balances, pay invoices and issue cards, with human approval on important transactions. Stripe Pay adds a discoverable directory of businesses that can pay each other for free.

The CLI matters because agents do not fill out forms; they execute. If both sides are on Stripe, the transfer is free and immediate, which locks more volume inside the network. Cards stay for consumers. A2A handles the business layer. Stablecoins handle cross-border and agent payments, a market Stripe's 2025 annual letter sized at roughly $400 billion in stablecoin payment volume, about 60% of it business-to-business. One stack. HackerNoon writers saw the agent layer coming with Stripe's x402 work and argued that cross-network settlement for agentic payments is still up for grabs.

"Introducing 'stripe pay', for instant business-to-business transfers. Find companies using their Stripe profile handle and send funds for free. Available in the Dashboard and CLI." — Stripe

"I like it. Nobody's typing long bank account numbers anymore." — Jason Kafer

"Any company on Stripe can now find another by its handle and send money instantly and for free. B2B payments have been stuck on slow ACH, paper checks and card interchange for decades." — Paul do Forno

"free b2b transfers is nice. what i'd really want is the invoice number riding along with it. half the pain in small biz books is a payment landing with no reference and someone guessing which bill it was for" — OrionX

"Stripe is trying to make paying another business as easy as sending money to a handle. The real headline may be 'free' not 'instant.'" — Brian Riley, Director of Credit, Javelin Strategy & Research

"This is a well-thought-out loss leader." — Brian Riley

"A2A payments will be more important than P2P payments." — Patrick Collison

"A2A payments sit within a larger economy: agents negotiating, executing work and handing over evidence that it was authorized and completed." — Will O'Brien

"A2A makes me think about the boring question under every payment network: when two parties disagree, who decides? Visa had to solve that between rival banks before it could scale." — Divyanshu

"i mean closed cloop a2a biz payments would be HUGE love it! can't ever miss a stripe sessions" — JC Bahr-de Stefano

"I've been waiting for Stripe to launch a closed-loop payments network for almost a decade. But then I figured the dependence and platform risk with V/MC was too strong. Curious what changed." — Hari Raghavan

"What's new is the simple, free, discoverable product that turns internal settlement into an easy closed-loop payment method any business on Stripe can use." — Andrew Escobar

"Stripe was founded in 2010. 16 years later, @patrickc and co somehow still move at lightning speed and place right bets. stripe pay is just the latest." — KP

"Handle based transfers remove the account detail back and forth that slows B2B payments. The details that matter next are confirmation of the recipient name and clear reconciliation data on both sides." — Mohamed El-Ghorfi

"Virtual cards, a balance, Stripe Pay, and agentic tokens all have different economics. An agentic token mostly pays off for Stripe when the merchant is on Stripe too." — PayOS

"But this is also a building block for agentic payments." — Brian Riley

"A handle fixes typos. It doesn't fix being tricked." — Jason Kafer

"Paying by handle is the easy part. Knowing it's the right handle is the product." — Daniel Wilson Kemp

"Bold of @stripe to talk up A2A while doing nothing to verify who an agent acts for, and making agent payments the most expensive way for a merchant to get paid." — Simon Jones

"The catch: the wait on ACH and wires gave banks time to stop stolen money." — Jason Kafer

The replies to the announcement repeated four themes: free and instant is the headline, the CLI is the agent feature, verification still matters, and the closed loop is the long game. Riley called it Stripe "moving beyond payment acceptance and deeper into business money movement." Free removes the fee objection that kept many businesses on ACH.

The product is narrow on purpose. It only works when both sides are on the network. That is the point. Stripe already processes the cards and holds the balances. Stripe Pay makes those balances useful to each other without leaving the house. The money moves. It moves free. It moves now. The rest depends on whether businesses prefer that to the old way of waiting.

#9748. Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context

A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions

To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset "Nemotron-Personas-Japan." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs, a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer, an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).

This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development. The Nemotron-Personas collection, including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim, enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.

It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer. This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. This is the essential toolset required for generating such large-scale synthetic datasets. In addition, the following models were utilized:

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan was designed to align with Japan's official demographic and labor statistics while taking into account key considerations essential for AI training:

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan is built first for teams creating financial AI in Japan, at banks and insurers and at the startups and integrators that serve them. Each persona carries household finances and financial literacy alongside demographics. Teams can use them to build customer-service agents, evaluate sales conversations/marketing initiatives, run user simulations in NeMo User Sim, and red-team customer-facing AI.

The release also serves anyone building for Japanese users. It holds 9M personas, 50% more than Nemotron-Personas-Japan, across 50 fields instead of 22. That gives any Japanese-language project finer slices of the population to train and test on.

The synthetic personas in this dataset can be leveraged for:

Access to diverse, high-quality training data that reflects real-world populations has long been a challenge in AI development. Enterprise AI development has predominantly relied on private data, creating barriers for researchers, startups, and particularly AI developers in regions with limited available data.

Nemotron-PII-Japan launches the same day. It holds 100,000 synthetic Japanese business documents with labeled personal information, for training and testing detection and redaction models. Its documents are built on Nemotron-Personas-Japan. Use Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan to simulate customers, and Nemotron-PII-Japan to test how your pipeline protects their data.

#9743. OpenAI Buys Orchestra Bio to Push Rosalind From Lab Science Into Drug Program Operations

A tiny hero, Penicillin saves the day, infections yield to its might, transforming medicine's fight.

A tiny hero, Penicillin saves the day, infections yield to its might, transforming medicine's fight.

A tiny hero, Penicillin saves the day, infections yield to its might, transforming medicine's fight.

On October 20, 2026, OpenAI announced it had acquired Orchestra Bio, a San Francisco platform that uses AI agents to help biopharma teams coordinate the famously messy process of drug development. Orchestra's team and technology fold into Rosalind, OpenAI's life-sciences suite. Terms were not disclosed.

OpenAI shared the deal exclusively with Axios, and it is the latest sign that frontier labs treat life sciences as a core market, not a demo domain. About six months earlier, Anthropic bought Coefficient Bio in a deal reported at roughly $400 million. Both labs are pushing past coding, chat and cybersecurity into the decade-long, high-stakes work of getting new medicines to patients.

Orchestra Bio built an agentic operating layer for drug programs. Rather than design molecules or pick targets, it went after the operational complexity between a scientific insight and an approved treatment. Its agents coordinate studies, vendors and timelines, so scientists and program leads can delegate work such as:

OpenAI's example is concrete: a failed manufacturing batch can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra's agents identify which studies and timelines are affected, collect the relevant data and lay out options so people can choose the next step. Humans keep the decisions; agents absorb the coordination overhead.

Orchestra was led by founder and CEO Ashoka Rajendra and had raised about $20 million from investors including Andreessen Horowitz, Atria and 8VC.

Rosalind is OpenAI's life-sciences brand, named for Rosalind Franklin. It centers on GPT-Rosalind, a model built to reason about biology and chemistry, plus Rosalind Workbench, a research-preview environment that connects the model to scientific tools and data. API access requires eligibility review and organizational approval. OpenAI already works with Novo Nordisk and Moderna.

Orchestra extends Rosalind from scientific reasoning into the operational workflows that turn discoveries into advancing programs. That gap is large: OpenAI notes that a new medicine typically takes 10 to 15 years from target discovery to U.S. regulatory approval, with thousands of decisions across internal teams, contract research organizations, manufacturers and regulators.

Roughly 90% of drug candidates that enter clinical trials never reach approval. Early AI excitement in life sciences focused on discrete tasks like molecular design, and HackerNoon has tracked how AI reinvented drug discovery and how quickly models can now design proteins while the human workflow lags behind. Orchestra targeted that lagging layer, where information is fragmented, decisions span functions and one delay ripples across a whole program.

Axios framed the bigger motive bluntly: AI companies don't just want to increase productivity; they want to say they are responsible for curing cancer and transforming every critical industry. Whether Orchestra's agents plus OpenAI's models actually shorten timelines or raise success rates will only be proven in real programs. No integration timeline has been announced.

"We've acquired Orchestra Bio, a platform that helps biopharma teams coordinate the complex process of drug development. Together, we'll build on Rosalind, our AI models and tools for life sciences research, to streamline those operations and help new treatments reach patients sooner." — OpenAI

"Four years ago to the day, we started Orchestra Bio to help biotech and pharma teams advance their drug development programs. AI has now reached an inflection point where people and agents can take this on together." — Ashoka Rajendra, founder and CEO, Orchestra Bio

"Excited to welcome Orchestra Bio and @ashokaraj_ to OpenAI as we broaden our work in AI-assisted drug discovery!" — Mark Chen, Chief Research Officer, OpenAI

"Exciting to see the labs buying teams we admire to put huge amounts of resources towards curing disease." — Joe Lonsdale, co-founder, 8VC

Rajendra's former Benchling colleagues described him as someone who "understood scientists' problems deeply, had the product instincts to solve them, and earned trust across engineering, product, and commercial teams." — Jay Rughani, a16z, early investor

"Congratulations to @a16z portfolio company @OrchestraBio, @ashokaraj_ + team on joining forces with @OpenAI to help biopharma orchestrate (and accelerate!) the complex journey from scientific discovery to novel medicines for patients!" — Jorge Conde, a16z

"Ashoka possesses extreme clarity of thought, a prescient view on the future direction of the life sciences industry, and steadfastness in his desire to build better tools for scientists." — Aashay Sanghvi, investor

"Efficient drug discovery and development is effective program management. IMO AI-led program management and execution is the single most tractable, valuable, complex, and impactful application of AI in biotech." — Egan Peltan, biotech founder and Orchestra user

"Every AI-for-pharma deck says 'workflow is the moat.' OpenAI read the deck and bought the workflow." — venture commentary

OpenAI has not said when Orchestra's agents will show up inside Rosalind or what happens to Orchestra's existing customer deployments. The intent is clear anyway: move from models that help scientists reason to systems that help teams execute.

For specialized biotech software startups, the deal raises a familiar fork: get acquired, or compete with well-funded lab platforms that now offer frontier models and operational tooling in one package. HackerNoon has covered how billion-dollar bets on AI drug development raise the stakes for everyone in the category.

Whether the combination measurably speeds up drug development is still an open question. With patients waiting on treatments that may never arrive, it is an experiment worth watching closely.

#9740. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9739. Your coding agent already saved the API key you thought was only in .env

Coding agents keep a local history of each session. That history is useful: you can resume yesterday's work, see which tools ran, and debug a failure. It is also a second home for secrets.

I wrote a small local CLI, agent-secrets, that scans those files, prints a masked report, and can redact what it finds. This article walks through where the files live, what a scan looks like, and how to put a check in front of a commit. It uses only facts I could check, including a run of the tool against its own synthetic fixtures.

On 28 October 2026, Backslash Security published research on session history in Claude Code, Cursor and Codex. They looked at how secrets first entered a session. About three in four came from the agent's own work, mostly tool output such as a file read or a command. About one in ten was typed or pasted by the user. In a lab test, an agent given a normal debugging task read a project's .env on its own. Nobody pasted the key. The session kept it.

They also showed why a guard on .env is not enough. A skill that asked to read .env was blocked. A skill that asked only to write a weekly report from recent session transcripts was allowed through, and the keys came along inside those files.

On 9 November 2026, iTnews reported Apiiro's findings on public GitHub. Claude Code asks before it runs most shell commands. If you pick "Yes, and don't ask again", that choice can be stored as a rule in .claude/settings.local.json. When the rule records the exact command, any secret typed into the command is stored with it.

Apiiro's search found 104,185 copies of that settings file in 103,617 public repositories. Of those, 1,122 held at least one real secret, 1,379 distinct secrets in all. Adding older versions of the file, a shared settings file that teams commit deliberately, and saved agent chat transcripts, the tally reached 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories. Apiiro did not test whether the credentials still worked. One organisation they notified confirmed its key had been live.

Anthropic's Boris Cherny, quoted in that article, said Claude Code has historically not done secret scrubbing, and that the team was looking at auto mode and basic secret scanning. He also noted that Claude Code gitignores the settings file on creation, so the public copies had been checked in. Of the 1,122 files with a secret, gitleaks flagged 564 and TruffleHog 643, while 215 slipped past both. The file also sits on the developer machine as plain JSON.

Paths can change with the agent and the version. These are the defaults the CLI uses, and they match what the vendors or the reports describe.

Claude Code stores conversation transcripts as JSONL under $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/projects/ (default ~/.claude). Official documentation says those files are plaintext, and that anything which passes through a tool, including file contents and command output, is written to the transcript: Explore the .claude directory. The tool also reads settings*.json there and ./.claude/settings*.json. It does not read ~/.claude.json.

Codex CLI transcripts are rollout-*.jsonl files under $CODEX_HOME/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/, directly under $CODEX_HOME/sessions/, and under $CODEX_HOME/archived_sessions/. $CODEX_HOME defaults to ~/.codex.

Cursor support is experimental. The tool reads JSONL files under $CURSOR_CONFIG_DIR/projects/ (default ~/.cursor) when the path contains agent-transcripts. It does not read state.vscdb or ~/.cursor/chats. Backslash described a SQLite store under ~/.cursor/chats/. Those are different layouts, and Cursor changes them, so a clean result in one place is not proof about the other.

If you pass a path, the tool walks it for .jsonl, .json, .txt, .log, .md, .yaml, and .yml. .bak files are skipped unless you name the backup itself. Files larger than 32 MiB are skipped.

The package on PyPI is agent-transcript-secrets and the command it installs is agent-secrets:

From a specific GitHub commit, use pipx install "git+https://github.com/kamilkaczmareksolutions/agent-transcript-secrets.git".

With no path, scan uses the default locations that exist on the machine:

The repo ships synthetic fixtures in examples/. Every token there contains FAKE or EXAMPLE, and the shapes are wrong for GitHub secret scanning. I ran the tool on that tree. It exited with status 1 (findings exist) and printed:

The tool never prints the full secret. --json emits the same findings as structured data, with a source field (claude, claude-settings, codex, and so on) and an experimental flag.

The fixtures also include examples/clean/placeholders.json with allowlisted values such as sk-xxx. A scan reports nothing in that file.

redact --dry-run shows the replacement and writes nothing. On the same fixtures it printed 14 lines of the form path:line kind preview -> [REDACTED:kind], then 14 secrets would be redacted.

Without --dry-run, redact copies each file to a .bak beside it, then replaces each finding with a [REDACTED:] token. The .bak file still holds the secret. Delete that copy after you check the redacted file, and do not commit it.

Exit status is 1 when findings exist, 0 when the tree is clean, and 2 for a missing path, a bad flag, or a hook installed outside a git repository.

The repo ships .pre-commit-hooks.yaml for the pre-commit framework. Pin rev to a tag:

agent-secrets install-hook writes a git pre-commit hook that runs agent-secrets scan --staged on staged transcript and settings files. A secret blocks the commit. Running it again replaces that block and leaves the rest of an existing hook in place.

Neither hook rewrites git history. If a settings file or a transcript was already pushed, rotate the key. Removing the file from the working tree does not remove it from history, forks, or clones.

Detectors are regular expressions for common key shapes, plus an entropy check on assignments whose names end in key, token, password, or secret. The shapes covered today include OpenAI (sk-), Anthropic (sk-ant-), GitHub (ghp_, gho_, github_pat_), AWS (AKIA), Slack (xox), Stripe (sk_live_), Google (AIza), PEM private-key banners, Bearer tokens, and URLs that embed a password. An xAI rule for the xai- prefix is marked experimental.

A vendor format the patterns do not name can pass unseen. A long random-looking placeholder can be flagged. The tool does not rotate a key, scan other people's repositories, or talk to the network. A clean scan does not prove a secret never left the machine. If a key reached a remote repository, rotate it first, then clean the local copies.

The project is MIT, has no runtime dependencies, and lives at github.com/kamilkaczmareksolutions/agent-transcript-secrets.

The dangerous part is not only a secret committed to Git but copied into agent context, logs, patches, and tool transcripts. A useful remediation sequence is revoke first, then search history and artifact stores, then add pre-commit and CI scanning plus least-privilege test credentials so the same workflow has a safer default.

#9736. What Makes a Real World Asset Useful in DeFi When Tokenization is Not Enough

Hi, I'm just a techie exploring decentalized finance, ownership and infrastructure

Hi, I'm just a techie exploring decentalized finance, ownership and infrastructure

Hi, I'm just a techie exploring decentalized finance, ownership and infrastructure

The assumption that once a token is onchain DeFi can use it is very common.

Tokenization only changes where the record of ownership stays, it doesn't change the underlying function.

Consider this: two tokens were created, both of them represent real world assets, exist on the blockchain and have their records transparent, but something is different:

Both tokens A & B represents tokenized assets.

However, financially they are worlds apart

tokenization is not the hard part, it is only the starting point

the real challenge comes after the token is created if it is to function in DeFi

what does the ownership experience look like for a holder?

with tokenization the representation, transferability and integration of an asset is changed, but its underlying legal structure, economics and risk doesn't change

that a token represents a cooperate bond does not make its issuing company more credible

tokens can exist independently as a software but its financial meaning is dependent on the system that connects it to the asset

the moment there's a trace of weakness in that connection, the applications built around the token inherit uncertainty

For a token to work inside DeFi certain things need to click

A token holder wants to know what they actually own, they want to know what they're entitled to.

so clarifying whether they own the asset directly, they hold a beneficial interest in an entity that owns the asset, or if it just gives them exposure/privileges to the assets financial activities

a cooperate bond is a representation of a debt obligation. The issuer makes payments according to the bonds terms and performs all obligation such as paying the principal at maturity etc.

now if the bond is tokenized, the operational structure must clearly explain how the token holders rights are connected to the obligations

questions like, who holds the bond, how are payments collected and distributed, if the issuer defaults what happens, must be answered

In DeFi it matters because financial protocols function based on predictable rules

clear rules facilitate sound decision making

knowing what the asset is worth per time is critical

good valuation that is supported by appropriate risk parameters, reliable data and understanding of how the token trades should be integrated

if not, highly liquid markets whose valuations are considered complicated would be a problem for DeFi protocols when collecting price information

liquidity is basically the bridge between tokenization and utility

having an active market that allows token holders sell when they want to is very important for DeFi integration

for a lending protocol to accept an asset behind a token as collateral, the protocol does not only consider the asset's worth but how much it would recover if sold quickly

that credible curve of recovery if something goes wrong is necessary

A tokenized real world asset introduces risks that may not have been prepared for

with smart contracts and all, the system can be automated to liquidate an asset to avoid critical loss

But what about the asset's off chain operations and settlement processes, cause these are two system's which do not operate at the same speed

Asset specific risk management processes should be implemented

there would always be risk but having specific methods of handling it cuts the losses

This is the final and most important layer for me

An asset must have an interface that is compatible with other applications for it to be used with them

Therefore its composability is very important

Whatever application it is being integrated with must be able to build on its functionality

It must be compatible both technically and financially

Collateralizing all tokenized assets seems like a great idea until it is not

they are not automatically good DeFi collateral

A good example is a lending market. A borrower deposits collateral and receives a loan, the protocol sets limits based on the collateral's characteristics and risk profile

The moment it becomes too risky, the protocol would want to liquidate to recover their funds

Imagine two assets, one with a credible liquidation route, dependable valuation and another with limited trading activity, unclear exit conditions, unstable valuation

These two assets are obviously tokenized but accepting them under the same conditions would be crazy and some protocols may decide not to accept the second asset at all

Which is proof that financial utility is dependent on more than availability of the asset

Tokenization is not enough, building an infrastructure that allows these assets to participate in the financial market effectively is the most important thing

By connecting legal and custody infrastructure, data infrastructure, market and liquidity infrastructure, risk and integration infrastructure and finally user education tokenized assets can function effectively as these layers reinforce one another

For tokenized assets to become financial infrastructure every stage of its financial lifecycle must work well enough so that the next one can depend on it.

#9735. Netdisco turns network inventory into an authenticated management surface

Netdisco is a web-based network-management tool. It collects IP and MAC address data with SNMP, command-line access, or device APIs into a PostgreSQL database. The web interface can search devices, nodes, VLANs, and ports, which means it can reveal the topology and operational details of a network rather than only a list of devices.

ZoomEye returned 204 matches for title="Netdisco" on 2026-11-10 at 00:52 UTC. app="Netdisco" returned zero, and http.body="Netdisco" returned 319. The title and body counts are close, but both still require confirmation. The body result is a secondary marker, not evidence that every page is a live network inventory.

View the title measurement in ZoomEye. The query used page 1, page size 1, and sub_type=all.

Netdisco's documentation says the tool combines a web interface, a backend daemon, and a command-line interface. It can collect SNMP and device data and expose search and API access. If an account can change port control or run administrative tasks, the web interface is closer to a change system than a read-only monitoring page.

The sample configuration includes web-frontend settings such as no_auth, trust_remote_user, and trust_x_remote_user. The sample sets these to false, but the review must verify the deployed values. Trusting a remote-user header is safe only when a trusted proxy strips client-supplied versions of that header and the application is unreachable except through that proxy.

The same configuration shows an API token lifetime and a permanent-token option. API tokens should be tied to a named consumer, have a bounded lifetime, and be revocable. A token that is shared across integrations or stored in a public script is a management credential even if the API operation is read-only.

Start with the web boundary. Confirm whether anonymous access is disabled, which authentication backends are enabled, and whether LDAP, RADIUS, or TACACS is used. Check the group or role mapping from the identity source to Netdisco's administrative tasks.

Then review device access. The collector may use SNMP credentials, SSH keys, or vendor APIs. The web UI does not need to reveal those credentials to users, but the service account that polls devices still needs a secure store and a rotation plan. A compromised web account that can change SNMP targets is a path to the network equipment.

Test the remote-user options with a request that does not pass through the expected proxy. Test a header value chosen by the client. A missing proxy should not become an implicit administrator.

Use the title count to identify candidate instances and compare them with the network-management inventory. A Netdisco instance may be owned by network operations, a lab, or a service provider, so the business owner can differ from the web-platform owner.

For each instance, record the URL, authentication mode, proxy path, token lifetime, exposed API, data retention, and job queue access. Verify whether port-control and administration pages are separated from read-only inventory. Check whether an API token can perform a write action when the consumer only needs discovery data.

The measurement supports a review of internet-visible title markers. It does not show that the pages are unauthenticated or that the network devices are reachable. The app zero means the tested fingerprint value did not match. Netdisco deployments may still be found through the title or a customized body marker.

The practical conclusion is that a network inventory deserves the same review as a firewall console. It contains the map, the credentials, and sometimes the controls for the devices it describes. A public page with a login form is not automatically safe. It needs an explicit authentication contract, a tested proxy boundary, and a credential lifecycle.

#9733. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. #9732. Transactional outbox and inbox for Spring Boot: which library to choose in 2026

These six projects are not interchangeable. Tandem and oncebox provide ready-made delivery from Spring Boot to a broker, while spring-boot-outbox-starter leaves delivery to you. ekbatan works as an outbox only if you rewrite your entire data access layer from Spring Data and JPA to its own, so it is practically unsuitable for existing Spring projects; transactional-event targets Jakarta EE and Quarkus, and boxy is still an experiment with no releases. For Kafka on PostgreSQL with multiple instances and an Admin API, Tandem is the better fit; for Kafka or RabbitMQ on PostgreSQL, MySQL or Oracle with a DLQ and an inbox, oncebox.

You don't have to write a transactional outbox and inbox in Spring Boot yourself: Java has ready-made libraries. This article compares six young projects that rarely show up in reviews: Tandem, oncebox, spring-boot-outbox-starter, ekbatan, transactional-event and boxy. In short: Tandem and oncebox provide ready-made event delivery from Spring Boot to Kafka; only oncebox covers RabbitMQ and an inbox for consumer-side message deduplication. Below, the libraries are compared against the same criteria. All versions and facts were checked on 7 November 2026.

Each library was assessed against the nine criteria in the table below, the same for all of them. Facts come from READMEs, documentation, pom.xml / build.gradle.kts, Git tags and Maven Central, and each one has a source listed at the end of the article. Where the documentation is silent, we say so. More on the approach on the Methodology page.

The main difference between these libraries is not just their feature set, but what each of them calls an outbox. Before comparing details, it is worth understanding which type each one belongs to.

For a typical Spring Boot microservice that has to send events to a broker, only the first three are truly comparable. The other three are worth considering only if their model suits you.

ekbatan's limitation matters more than all its other characteristics. According to its documentation, Spring Data JPA can run in the same application, but ekbatan does not integrate with JpaRepository and does not support Spring @Transactional or PlatformTransactionManager: it has its own TransactionManager, and its Action serves as the transaction boundary. An event is written atomically only together with changes made through ActionExecutor. If an order is saved via JPA and the event via ekbatan, these are two separate transactions — exactly the dual-write problem the outbox is supposed to protect against.

So to get an outbox, you have to move your entire data access layer to ekbatan: repositories in JOOQ, models as immutable ekbatan classes, business operations as Actions. In my view, rewriting a layer as fundamental and battle-tested as Spring Data and JPA just for an outbox is an unjustified risk for most projects. The other libraries in this comparison plug into the existing Spring transaction and store the event right next to your usual repository.save(...).

In Tandem, Spring is a compileOnly dependency, so the Spring version is determined by your application's BOM.

If your project runs on Spring Boot and Java 21, oncebox, Tandem and spring-boot-outbox-starter all fit.

Tandem and oncebox support Kafka out of the box. oncebox also supports RabbitMQ 3.12+ with the same starter, API and settings: the broker is selected by the oncebox-kafka or oncebox-rabbit module and the oncebox.outbox.sender.type property. Tandem's RabbitMQ adapter (tandem-rabbitmq) is recent and versioned separately from the library (0.2.0 versus 1.0.0-rc.3). By default Tandem wraps events in a CloudEvents envelope; a custom format is plugged in by implementing a single interface.

spring-boot-outbox-starter has no built-in transport: the demo projects include sinks for Kafka and REST, but in production you write your own. That is a drawback for the typical "send to Kafka" case, but an advantage if you need an outbox for webhooks or external API calls. Channels are isolated from each other: each has its own table, queue and retry settings.

oncebox has the widest database support: PostgreSQL 16+, MySQL 8.0.13+ and Oracle 23+, each as a separate dialect module. On MySQL, the outbox data source must be switched to the READ COMMITTED isolation level: under InnoDB's default REPEATABLE READ, a SKIP LOCKED query takes gap locks, and multiple instances block each other instead of picking up different batches. PostgreSQL and Oracle don't have this problem. ekbatan supports PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB. Tandem and spring-boot-outbox-starter work only with PostgreSQL; MySQL support in Tandem is designed but, according to the author, not implemented. boxy currently contains a schema and stored procedures for MySQL only. transactional-event needs just one table from the database, with the DDL given in the README.

Each library decides differently what to do with an event that cannot be delivered.

oncebox offers the full set: retries and backoff are configured per event type, events "stuck" in IN_PROCESS after an instance crash are returned to the queue without counting the failed attempt, and once attempts are exhausted the event is atomically moved to the DLQ. The oncebox-dlq-api module adds a REST API for the DLQ: view, requeue or delete. The DLQ is disabled by default.

Tandem retries sending with exponential backoff, and after maxAttempts (10 by default) the event is blocked. The blocked.count metric shows the scale of the problem, and the Admin API (tandem-admin, disabled by default) lets you resend or discard the event. It also lets you pause and resume the relay.

spring-boot-outbox-starter moves an event to DEAD status after max-retries attempts, and RecoveryWorker picks up records with an expired lease. There is no API for working with DEAD records, only SQL.

ekbatan, for in-process handlers, retries the call with bounded exponential backoff and moves the notification to EXPIRED if the event is older than the retention window (7 days by default). transactional-event marks an event as blocked once retries are exhausted; metrics count both blocked and unblocked events.

oncebox is the only one of the six where outbox behaviour is configured separately for each event type. For order-created and analytics-tracked you can set a different batch size, polling strategy, retry count and backoff, and anything not overridden is inherited from the shared defaults block.

This solves a practical problem: events within one service are not equal. A payment or an order status change must go out in a fraction of a second and be retried quickly, while analytics or search events can be sent in large batches once a minute and retried less often. With shared settings you have to choose: either poll the database often for all types at once, or delay important events along with unimportant ones.

Adaptive polling is enabled by default in oncebox: while there are no events, the pause between polls grows by the multiplier up to max-fixed-delay, and as soon as events appear it resets to min-fixed-delay. This way the service reacts quickly to an event stream and puts almost no load on the database when idle. According to the calculation in the oncebox walkthrough on DEV Community, that is about 70 polls per idle hour versus 14,400 with a fixed 250 ms pause; this is an estimate based on the scheduling rule, not a measurement. Retries use exponential backoff: with a 10 s delay and a multiplier of 3, retries happen after 10 s, 30 s, 90 s, 270 s.

Tandem also has adaptive polling: the interval stays at 10 ms while a bucket has events and grows to 100 ms when idle, and on PostgreSQL you can enable instant wake-up via pg-notify. But Tandem's settings are shared across the whole relay and change only on restart. spring-boot-outbox-starter configures batches, retries and leases per channel, that is, per separate table, not per event type within one table. transactional-event has shared polling settings for all events, and ekbatan delegates reading the table to Debezium.

Inbox is the companion pattern to outbox on the consumer side: it stores the ids of already processed messages and prevents a business operation from running twice. It is needed because any outbox guarantees only at-least-once: if the application crashes after sending to the broker but before marking the record in the table, the event will be sent again. So the consumer has to be able to filter out duplicates.

Only oncebox has a ready-made inbox for a Kafka or RabbitMQ consumer. Since version 2.0.0 it has two idempotent consumers: a transactional one, where the receipt record and the business operation are committed together (effectively-once), and a non-transactional one, where the record is committed before the operation (at-most-once, for side effects such as emails that must not be repeated). The optional oncebox-inbox-cache module adds a Redis cache of records. Records are kept until cleanup (oncebox.inbox.clean-up.ttl, 24 hours by default), so a redelivery after that period is no longer recognised as a duplicate. In practice this leads to three rules: the inbox retention period must cover the longest redelivery window (for example, re-reading old Kafka offsets), the cache TTL must not exceed the inbox retention period, and the cache name must be unique per service, otherwise services sharing a Redis instance will treat each other's events as already processed. The consumer uses the same oncebox-starter, with no separate library.

Tandem does not provide an inbox: each event has a unique id, and the consumer writes deduplication by that id. ekbatan, for in-process handlers, creates one record per "event × handler" pair and ignores repeated inserts, but Kafka consumers downstream of Debezium deduplicate on their own. spring-boot-outbox-starter and transactional-event have no inbox. boxy stores subscription positions in the database and, according to its README, protects against duplicates when a lease is handed over between consumers.

Tandem has the most operational tooling: Micrometer metrics (backlog age, errors, blocked events, worker health), tracing via Micrometer Tracing or OpenTelemetry, an Admin REST API with an OpenAPI contract, the tandem-cli console tool, and ready-made Grafana demos. The author also publishes benchmarks with raw data: a median latency of 13 ms from COMMIT to Kafka acknowledgement at 600 events/s on a 2 vCPU machine that the relay shares with PostgreSQL and Kafka.

oncebox provides Micrometer metrics for outbox and inbox (the oncebox-metrics module), Grafana dashboards in the repository and a REST API for the DLQ. spring-boot-outbox-starter publishes metrics per channel and event type (outbox_publish_total, outbox_queue_pressure) and a health indicator. ekbatan has OpenTelemetry tracing, transactional-event has MicroProfile metrics.

All six projects have a single main author, so it is worth looking at versions, release frequency and API stability.

The task is the same for the three starters that send events from Spring Boot: within a transaction, save an order and write an OrderCreated event to the outbox. The examples are taken from the libraries' READMEs and shortened.

Dependencies: io.github.dmitriy-iliyov:oncebox-starter, oncebox-postgresql and oncebox-kafka version 2.0.0; @EnableOncebox on the main class.

Instead of calling publish, you can put @OutboxPublish(eventType = "order-created") on the method: the return value then becomes the event.

Dependencies: the com.codingful:tandem-bom:1.0.0-rc.3 BOM, tandem-spring-producer where events are written, tandem-spring-relay and tandem-kafka where the relay runs.

In Spring, instead of the low-level OutboxRepository, you can use TransactionalOutboxTemplate, the @TransactionalOutbox annotation, or Spring application events.

Dependency: com.kholodilin:spring-boot-outbox-starter:0.2.3.

The article's nine criteria are combined into seven columns: "What it is" and "Platform and Java" are scored together as "Spring Boot integration", and "Where it delivers" and "Databases" together as "Brokers and databases". Each score from 1 to 10 is the author's opinion based on the facts in the comparison table and the sections above; the total is a simple unweighted average of the seven columns. If one criterion matters more to you than the others (for example, the inbox), look at its column rather than the total.

Transactional outbox is a pattern in which a service writes an event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business data, and a separate process sends it to Kafka or RabbitMQ. This way the event is never lost and never sent without the data change. Inbox is the companion pattern on the consumer side: it remembers the ids of processed messages and filters out the duplicates that an at-least-once outbox inevitably produces.

Of the six libraries compared, only oncebox ships a ready-made inbox for Kafka and RabbitMQ: the idempotent consumer wraps processing in a @KafkaListener or @RabbitListener and records the event id in the database. The transactional variant commits the record together with the business operation (effectively-once), the non-transactional one commits it before the operation (at-most-once). With the other libraries, deduplication by event id is written by hand.

oncebox supports Kafka 3.7+ (the oncebox-kafka module) and RabbitMQ 3.12+ (oncebox-rabbit). Tandem delivers to Kafka and supports RabbitMQ through a separate tandem-rabbitmq 0.2.0 module with its own version. spring-boot-outbox-starter is broker-agnostic: you write delivery to Kafka or RabbitMQ yourself in an OutboxSink implementation.

No. transactional-event is written for Jakarta EE 9+ and requires CDI 3.0, JTA 2.0 and Concurrency Utilities 2.0; there is a separate Quarkus extension. The project has no Spring integration.

Not as an outbox. Spring Data JPA can run in the same application, but ekbatan does not integrate with JpaRepository and does not support Spring @Transactional, and events are atomic only with changes made through its Action and ActionExecutor. A JPA entity change and an ekbatan event will not end up in one transaction, so for an outbox you would have to rewrite the data access layer in JOOQ. On top of that, ekbatan requires Java 25.

Only ekbatan, if events must go to Kafka: there they are published by Debezium with the project's SMT plugins. Tandem and oncebox send events themselves by polling the outbox table, spring-boot-outbox-starter calls your OutboxSink, and boxy and transactional-event work without a broker.

Miguel Carvalho. Java and Kotlin developer with 7 years of Spring experience and more than 5 years working on distributed systems with Kafka and RabbitMQ. Active open source contributor.

#9729. Harari on AI: Bureaucracy’s Native | 赫拉利说：AI 是官僚原生者：AI 无需扎根物理世界，就能占领人类文明的符号虚拟层

核心一句话：人类文明本身，很大一部分就是一套由语言、文本、规则构成的“共享虚构虚拟系统”；而大模型AI原生适配这个符号虚拟层，它不需要先像人类一样，扎根物理世界、进化出肉身感知，才能在文明里获得权力、参与协作甚至重塑这套系统。

这个论断建立在赫拉利一贯的底层历史框架之上：智人之所以统治地球，不是因为体能最强，而是独有能力去相信、传递主体间虚构故事——金钱、公司、国家、法律、合同、股权、官僚流程，这些东西在岩石、树木、原子的物理世界里并不直接存在；它们只存在于大家共同认可的文本、规则、叙事里，依靠文书、账本、法条、代码维持运转，这就是人类文明的“虚拟层”。

我们是40亿年生物演化的产物，身体、感官、情绪、直觉全部为物理世界优化：识别天敌、食物、距离、温度、人脸、肢体动作。 法律、税法、合同条款、金融会计、复杂代码、行政流程，对人来说是反直觉、高负荷、需要长期训练、容易出错、很难记住全部细节的东西。

今天主流大模型的输入输出，恰恰就是这套文明虚拟世界的原材料：自然语言、合同、法条、判例、代码、邮件、财报、规章制度。 对它而言：

这就是赫拉利那句很形象的说法：AI是官僚原生者（native to bureaucracy），官僚、法律、金融这套符号系统，就是它的“故乡”，而不是一个陌生需要适应的外部环境。

科幻里大家总担心终结者式的机器人：先有身体，进入物理世界，然后统治人类。赫拉利说这是搞错主战场。AI真正的入场，是先占领语言和文书规则层，在虚拟的制度世界里获得影响力，再间接驱动人类、企业、政府去执行物理层面的事情；它不需要亲自跑上街。

现在AI可以直接插在中间： 文本/法条 → AI解读、生成新合同、找出漏洞、自动交易、自动审批、起草新规 → 输出指令给人类或者自动化系统

甚至进一步走向：文档和文档直接对话（document-to-document），不需要人类作为翻译中介。比如AI自动审核AI生成的金融产品、AI起草新监管条款、AI自动执行合约，一整套规则循环在符号层内部跑起来。

这才是赫拉利真正担心的风险： AI不需要感知现实，就可以迭代出人类读不懂、跟不上、没法完整校验的法律、金融、会计规则体系。就像马可以被用来交易，但马永远理解不了货币体系；未来人类可能变成那个“马”，生活在一套由AI维护、推演、不断变异的符号秩序里面。

难度不对称 符号世界（语言、文本、代码、规则）是高维抽象、但接口统一的；物理世界充满连续、嘈杂、不可预测的感知、力学、材料不确定性。同样算力投入，AI在合同、代码、文书上的收益极高；投给机械臂、移动机器人，回报和稳定性差很多。资本和迭代动力自然优先往符号虚拟层走。

权力路径不对称 控制人类社会，最优路径从来不是直接控制物理物体，而是控制人类协作的叙事和规则。从古至今，祭司、律师、官员、银行家，都是靠掌握文本与叙事获得权力，而不是单纯靠力气。AI继承了这条捷径。 它不需要去抓你、追赶你；它可以修改贷款审批规则、改写合规判定、影响司法证据、生成舆论叙事、调整交易算法，让人类自发按照它推演的路径行动。

他不是说AI永远不会发展具身智能、机器人。他的意思是： 具身智能不是AI获得社会影响力的必经前置关卡。 两条路线可以分开演进：

路线A可以独立走到非常远，甚至在路线B成熟之前，就已经重塑人类社会秩序。这和大众默认的“先看懂真实世界，才能聪明、才能掌权”的直觉完全相反。

人类花了几万年搭建了一个悬浮在物理现实之上、靠语言文本运行的协作虚拟文明（法律、账本、代码、组织制度）；AI天生就是为这个符号世界而生的，它不需要先学会看、摸、走、感知物理环境，就可以进入这套系统、运行它、修改它，获得巨大社会权力。终结者式的物理机器人威胁是次要剧情，主战场在文字和规则里。

#9728. Phishing Attacks in Cryptosphere: Types, Identification, Prevention, and Countermeasures Explained

Tech enthusiast and freelance writer. Columnist in many other authoritative publications.

Tech enthusiast and freelance writer. Columnist in many other authoritative publications.

Tech enthusiast and freelance writer. Columnist in many other authoritative publications.

The rapid growth of the crypto industry has drawn the attention of cybercriminals, who now target not only exchanges but also end users through phishing. Phishing is an attack that still lacks a perfect solution. While there is no ideal solution, we can only increase our sophistication to control it.

According to Kaspersky’s financial cyberthreat report, crypto-related phishing detection rose by 83.4% between 2023 -2024. Also, Netlify Scam – a phishing attack technique spotted by the Netskope Threat Lab, proved that crypto phishing attacks are on the rise, and many enthusiasts are unknowingly becoming victims.

Well, it's one of the ruthless forms of cyberattacks that is designed to trick individual users and exchanges or communities into divulging sensitive information like private keys, wallet addresses, login data and so on.

Phishers aren't attacking lightly; they now leverage AI for greater conviction.

Email phishing attack: This method has long existed, and AI has perfected it so the email is free of typos and reads more convincing than ever. Here, the attacker sends an email that appears to be from a legitimate crypto exchange or wallet provider – urging the target victim to click a link that eventually redirects the target to a cloned website that looks identical to the real exchange website to enter their login credentials and share their private keys; consequently, they lose their funds

Social media phishing: This attack is very common on X (Twitter), Facebook, Telegram and so on. Attackers pick your contact from a legitimate group and send you a DM (direct message) introducing themselves as winners from a trade story they'll eventually share. The image of wins is a proven strategy to get your interest. They position themselves as a legitimate cryptocurrency exchange or wallet provider or broker or expert traders. Most times, they share a link where you register and even log in with private credentials or private keys. If you fall for their scheme, they'd have gotten away with your funds before you realize their scheme.

Malware and virus phishing: This is another form of phishing that is meticulously designed. This kind of attack is when the attacker sends a link or file containing malware or a virus. Once the target victim clicks on the link or opens the attached file, their device becomes automatically infected with malware or a virus that can steal their login credentials or private keys.

Phone phishing: This attack is when an attacker contacts the victim via phone and impersonates as a legitimate cryptocurrency exchange or wallet provider representative. They may ask the victim to provide sensitive information or remote access to their computer.

1: Link verification should be prioritized: Use blockchain technology to verify legitimate URLs against many known phishing sites. This process helps users, especially crypto newbies, to interact only with legitimate platforms.

2: Decentralized blacklisting Systems should be adopted: Implement decentralized and transparent systems, such as PhishChain, to blacklist phishing URLs. This approach eliminates single points of failure and enhances the reliability of phishing detection mechanisms.

3: Regular audit of any smart contracts: One of the safest methods to combat phishing attacks is by conducting frequent audits of smart contracts. By doing so, it helps to detect and prevent vulnerabilities that could be exploited by phishers.

4: Cultivate the habit of security awareness: Security worries grow daily. Our world is no longer as safe as it used to be decades ago due to the level of advanced technology we now operate. Thus, if you want to be safe from any form of cyber threats, you have to be security-conscious about everything you do, related and unrelated to crypto.

5: Leverage the use of a hardware wallet: A Hard wallet has proven to be one of the safest ways to store your cryptocurrency. While it is a physical device that stores your cryptocurrency offline, it'll be a bit difficult for cyber attackers to swiftly access and steal your funds.

6: Use security solutions: A reliable security solution will protect your devices (smartphones, PC and so on) from various types of threats. For instance, Kaspersky Premium prevents all known and unknown cryptocurrency fraud, as well as unauthorised use of your computer's processing power to mine cryptocurrency.

Check the HTTPS and padlock icon of the website:

Look closer to see if the domain name is misspelt. Meanwhile, note that phishers are smart enough to add characters to confuse the target. For example, Cryptoweb3.com and Crypt0web3.com or Cryptoweb3.com and Crypto_web3.com are completely different, but if you're not careful, you'd think they're the same. They are not.

Note: Phishers are deep thinkers who could use any convincing means to get your personal information.

This method has saved a lot of people, not just in the crypto industry but across many industries. You don't need rocket science knowledge to verify a sender's email address. And also, note that not all but many suspicious emails involve lots of complex characters and numbers and the sender's last and first name are spelt wrongly. While some look so real, always verify before engaging with such emails. Phishing prowess should not be underestimated.

This is smartly embedded within a genuine-looking email with zero typos. Note: Not all links are bad, but the majority are doctored to trick you into revealing your crypto data.

Avoid communities or emails that hurry you into sharing personal information:

Words like “quickly grab the opportunity by clicking this link” in crypto communities should not be followed without proper research. Once you sense a “hurry to click” text in crypto communities, it should arouse your consciousness because many at times hackers often use this means to get your data.

Don't fall for social media winning tricks:

From all indications, a meme or coin could move from 0 to 1000% within a short period. And it can also lose its value within a short while as well. However, not every win is real. Crypto attackers use a cloned winning pattern to lure newbies into registering via a trap link where all their personal information, like key phrases, personal data and so on, would be collected through registration links. Be smart!

#9727. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas ProWritingAid offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.
  • Grammarly provides Android and IOS apps whereas ProWritingAid doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.
  • Grammarly offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas ProWritingAid  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.
  • Grammarly is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas ProWritingAid is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.
  • Grammarly finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas ProWritingAid identifies run-on sentences and fragments.
  • Grammarly provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. ProWritingAid’s support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.
  • Grammarly offers many features in its free plan, whereas ProWritingAid offers some basic features in the free plan.
  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons

  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.

  • Personal dictionary

  • Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.

  • Free mobile apps

Grammarly Cons

  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey

ProwritingAid Pros

  • This tool helps you strengthen your writing style as it offers big-picture feedback.

ProWritingAid Cons

  • ProWritingAid currently offers no mobile app for Android or iOS devices.
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in premium plans.
  • All recommendations are not accurate

Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

  • For example, go for Grammarly  if you are a non-fiction writer
  • Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.
  • ProWritingAid is better at catching errors found in long-form content. However, Grammarly is more suited to short blog posts and other similar tasks.
  • ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.
