#9724. I benchmarked my malware scanner against GuardDog on 15 fresh samples of npm and PyPI malware. Here is every result, including the losses.

Every few weeks another npm or PyPI package turns out to steal tokens on install. The usual advice is "check before you install", but few people have a tool that does the checking, and fewer know how well that tool works.

I build vetcode, an open-source scanner for malicious packages, supply-chain attacks and leaked secrets. Before telling anyone to use it, I wanted to know how it compares with the best free tool in this space. That tool is GuardDog from Datadog. A recent paper (NPMAnalysis) ranked it first among 13 npm malware detectors.

This post covers how I measured, every result I got, and where vetcode still loses.

Data. Malicious npm packages come from NPMAnalysis. Malicious PyPI packages come from the Datadog malicious-software-packages dataset. The clean side is real, popular packages from the npm and PyPI registries.

Fresh samples only. Each run draws a random sample with a new seed. I tune rules on one seed, then confirm on a seed that has never been looked at. Every number below comes from a confirmation seed. A scanner tuned and scored on the same samples will always look good.

Same packages for both tools. Both scanners read exactly the same tarballs. Nothing is installed or executed; both tools only read files.

GuardDog gets its best verdict. GuardDog has no single yes/no answer, so I scored it four ways: any issue, any threat rule, risk score ≥ 5, and risk score ≥ 7. It is credited with whichever gives the best F1 on each sample. vetcode is scored one way only: "flagged at severity high or above".

False alarms matter more than they look. A tool that flags 1 in 5 popular packages gets switched off.

vetcode wins five of eight. GuardDog wins three, by 0.1 to 1.1 F1 points. Two of its wins are on the small 300-package samples, where one package moves F1 by about half a point.

The more consistent difference is false alarms. vetcode flags 1.3–3.4% of clean packages; GuardDog flags 2.4–6.4%. On the latest 1,000-package sample that is 8 clean packages against 32.

Here the gap is clear. GuardDog's PyPI rules fire on many ordinary packages: 20–30% of popular packages get flagged at its best setting.

Seed 15 is the one I learned most from. GuardDog caught more malware there (79.3% vs 76.7%). Two kinds of package were behind the gap:

I added rules for both, and recall went back above GuardDog's on the next fresh sample.

Malware authors know scanners read source code, so they rewrite it. I wrote a script that rewrites caught samples the same way, without running anything. Then I checked how many each tool still catches. The table shows the share of previously caught samples still caught:

vetcode decodes these tricks before its rules run, and it labels what it found "(hidden)". It does this statically: joins split strings, decodes escapes, rebuilds character-code strings, reverses reversed ones, and unpacks base64 or zlib payloads up to three layers deep.

Building this benchmark also found a real bug: one of vetcode's own regexes could hang for minutes on a 500 KB base64 line. Measuring hostile input finds things that clean input never does.

Public datasets are full of 2021–2023 typosquats. Newer techniques are rare in them, so I keep a separate set of 15 hand-built cases from recent campaigns. Each one sits next to a clean look-alike that must not be flagged:

vetcode catches 15 of 15 with no false alarms on the look-alikes.

On the same 30 PyPI packages (659 MB), GuardDog took 1,104 seconds and vetcode 299. Since then vetcode has become another third faster. It has zero dependencies: Node 18+ and nothing else.

Scan a project, a package you are about to install, or a repo you just cloned:

It also runs as an MCP server and as a GitHub Action that comments on pull requests.

Every script used here is in bench/. If you run it and get different numbers, or find a malicious package vetcode misses, please open an issue. That is the most useful thing you can send me.

vetcode is MIT-licensed and part of OpenYard, a small community of open-source projects.

If you want to fix a Make webhook not receiving data, a seven-point checklist finds exactly where the data stops — no guessing, no code. Run the checks in order, from the outside in, and the first one that fails is your break.

Disclosure: Some links below are affiliate links, meaning StackScale may earn a commission at no extra cost to you.

Get started with Make here: https://www.make.com/en/register?pc=stackscale&affiliateSource=devto

A webhook is a URL waiting for data. When nothing lands, Make cannot tell you why — the break could be in the sending app, the URL, the payload, or the scenario, and each one looks identical: silence. So do not guess. Check, in order, from the outside in.

Fire a test request like this one and watch what Make receives:

Check three things about the bundle that arrives: it is valid JSON, the content type is right, and no field arrives blank. If any of those fail, the webhook can look fine while the data is broken.

Run the checklist and the webhook receives again — 200 OK, data flowing, no guessing. If a silent webhook has bitten you before, run the checks in this order next time and the break will name itself.

#9718. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9716. Why Apache returned 502 for our Go uploads

An oversized upload should give someone a useful rejection. In our case, the browser received "Upload failed: 502" even though the Go handler had a file-too-large response. The affected site was RadarMakers, a free launch platform for indie makers, with Apache forwarding uploads to Go.

The interesting part was the difference between the application response and the response that reached the browser. The workaround checks the declared request length before parsing multipart data, attempts a bounded discard of an oversized body, then writes the rejection.

This account comes from the current handler and its Git history. The earlier failure is documented there; I have not reproduced it for this article. The code explains a specific workaround, with limits that matter as much as the happy path.

The failure was not simply that the application rejected a large file. The browser saw a 502 from Apache when the Go server reset the connection while the proxy was still forwarding the body. A direct request to the API had produced the handler response instead. That distinction is why the investigation followed the request across both hops.

Start a similar incident by capturing the browser response, the proxy error log, and the application log for the same request window. Compare a request sent through the public route with one sent directly to the service in a controlled environment. Keep the same method, headers, body, and authentication state. If the two paths differ, inspect how the proxy handles upstream resets and unread request bytes before changing the application status code.

This case record does not claim that every 502 during an upload has this cause. A proxy can return a gateway error for many upstream failures. Here the repository comment identifies the reset during body forwarding, and the recorded comparison showed a different response on the direct path. Those are the facts behind this particular workaround.

The handler checks the declared Content-Length before wrapping the body or calling the multipart parser. When that value exceeds the request threshold, it takes a rejection path without parsing the form. This avoids spending image parsing work on a request that the server already intends to reject.

The header is only an early signal. A client can omit the length or send a value that does not describe the bytes that arrive. The source therefore keeps a second guard with http.MaxBytesReader before ParseMultipartForm. The Go documentation describes that reader as a request body limit that returns a MaxBytesError after a read crosses the configured size, and says it may tell the response writer to close the connection if possible.

The two checks answer different questions. The first decides whether the declared size already exceeds the limit and can be rejected before parsing. The reader limit protects the path where the header cannot make that decision. Neither check proves that the image is safe to decode. Content length limits transport size; image validation has separate responsibilities.

On the declared oversized path, the handler attempts to discard up to five times the body limit. With the current constant, that is a maximum read attempt of 25 MiB. The io.CopyN call writes to io.Discard, so these bytes are consumed for connection handling and are not stored as an upload.

A bounded drain is a tradeoff, not a universal recipe. Reading a portion of a rejected body can give a proxy a chance to finish forwarding bytes already in flight, but an unbounded read would let an oversized client keep the handler occupied for an arbitrary amount of data. The cap makes the maximum discard request explicit. The code ignores the returned byte count and error, then writes the 400 response, so it does not claim that every oversized body was fully consumed.

The comparison is important when changing the constants. Raising the file limit also changes the allowed request size and may change the maximum drain if the multiplier stays fixed. Increasing only the drain cap changes how much rejected traffic the handler may read. These values should be reviewed separately and tested with the proxy configuration that actually fronts the service.

HTTP request bodies can arrive without a useful declared size. The handler still wraps the body with MaxBytesReader, so the multipart parse cannot consume an unbounded body through this path. The same fallback also matters if the declared value is smaller than the bytes actually read. The header check is therefore an optimization and early rejection, not the sole security boundary.

A test suite should cover both known and unknown lengths. For a declared body above the threshold, assert that the early branch returns the intended status and message without parsing a multipart field. For a body whose declared size does not cross the threshold but whose actual bytes exceed it, assert that the reader limit controls the result. If the request uses chunked transfer, exercise the actual server and proxy path because middleware and proxy buffering can affect which component sees the limit first.

Avoid writing a test that only calls the handler directly and then declaring the production 502 fixed. The original difference occurred across Apache and Go. A direct handler test can verify the application branch, but it cannot verify how a deployed proxy handles a reset. Keep those claims separate in test names and release notes.

The configured limit is applied to the request body and multipart parsing. After the file is read, the handler also decodes and re-encodes the image. A compressed image can represent far more pixels than its byte size suggests. That is why the code checks the image header before decoding all pixels, and why the comment explains the risk of an extremely large image dimension.

The header buffer in the handler is 64 KiB. io.ReadFull attempts to fill that buffer, while treating EOF and unexpected EOF as conditions that can still leave a usable short header. The checkImage call receives only the bytes actually read. If the header cannot be parsed, the handler returns a client error before calling sanitizeImage.

A request size limit and a dimension check protect different resources. The first bounds incoming body bytes. The second rejects an image whose decoded dimensions would require unreasonable memory. Re-encoding then creates a cleaned output from pixels rather than copying the original file bytes. These operations should remain independently visible in code review because a change to one does not remove the need for the others.

The current allowlist accepts PNG, JPG, JPEG, and GIF after lowercasing the filename extension. SVG is deliberately absent because it is an active document format when served from the same origin. WebP is also absent because this implementation uses the standard library image path and re-encodes supported pixels. The allowlist is not a statement that every file with an accepted suffix is valid; the image decoder and sanitizer still inspect its contents.

A filename suffix is user supplied. It should not be treated as proof of the media type. The handler reads a header, checks it against the expected extension, seeks back to the start, reads the file, and sanitizes the decoded content. If a new format is added, test mismatched suffixes, malformed headers, oversized dimensions, and the final saved output. Also confirm that the chosen decoder and encoder remove metadata that should not be retained.

Instrument the rejection path without logging the file contents or sensitive request data. Useful fields include the route, the outcome category, whether the declared size crossed the threshold, and whether the request had a usable length. Avoid recording raw filenames if they may contain personal data. A counter by outcome can help detect a burst of rejected uploads, but it cannot show whether the proxy delivered the intended response. For that, compare proxy status and application status in a request trace with a safe correlation identifier.

Keep the logs explicit about boundaries. The application can record that it wrote a 400 response. The proxy log can record what it returned to the client. If those values differ, the path between the two is the subject of the next investigation. Do not collapse them into one field called upload status.

The existing order expresses a set of useful invariants. Authentication is checked before upload processing. Declared oversized bodies are rejected before multipart parsing. Other bodies are wrapped in a byte limit. The multipart form must contain the expected file field. The extension must be allowed. Image data is checked from its header before a full decode. The source bytes are re-read from the start for sanitization, then only the cleaned result is saved.

When refactoring, preserve the ordering or explain which property has changed. A helper that moves parsing above the length check may reintroduce the expensive path. A helper that copies original bytes to disk may preserve metadata or unsafe content. A broader format list may bypass the established sanitizer. Write a test for each boundary that matters rather than asserting only that a valid PNG succeeds.

The documented workaround is deliberately narrow. It changes the oversized declared-length path so the handler can attempt a capped drain before writing its intended response. It does not claim to solve every proxy timeout, every malformed multipart form, or every malicious image. That narrow description is more useful to the next person debugging a similar symptom than a general promise that uploads are now safe.

The threshold chart shows the exact request limit and drain ceiling read from internal/handler/upload.go. The format chart counts the extensions in the source allowlist: four accepted suffixes and two explicitly absent formats discussed in the code comments. These are implementation facts, not measurements of traffic or an estimate of risk. The diagrams already in the asset folder remain useful for request flow and the branch order; the charts add the actual values that a reader may want to compare with a proposed code change.

Before changing either number, rerun the relevant tests and inspect the deployment proxy limits, upload timeout, and body buffering configuration. This repository record documents the Go handler and its comments. It does not establish the settings of every reverse proxy or the behavior of every client.

Commit 33cb05b, dated August 26, 2026, records an oversized upload returning 502 through Apache and 400 when sent directly to the API. That comparison is the historical observation. It places the discrepancy between the direct API response and the response delivered through the proxy.

The handler comments describe the mechanism: the body limit was crossed while Apache was still forwarding the upload, the Go connection reset, and Apache answered the browser with a bare 502. The intended rejection lost its useful explanation along the way.

That is the documented behavior of this deployment. It should not be read as a universal rule that every call to MaxBytesReader immediately resets a connection. The Go documentation for MaxBytesReader describes a reader that errors when reads exceed the limit and, where possible, tells the response writer to close the connection afterward.

The distinction matters when investigating a similar symptom. A browser's status describes what arrived at the browser. Reading the handler's error branch alone does not establish that its response survived the proxy path.

The size constant remains small and explicit. Excerpt from internal/handler/upload.go:

The expression is 5 MiB. The comment and user-facing message say MB, but the binary count is what the code enforces. More precisely, this is a request body limit. A multipart upload includes framing and fields as well as the file, so it is not an exact allowance of 5 MiB for image bytes alone.

The handler first checks authentication and returns 401 if claims are absent. The length decision discussed here happens after that check. It is not a description of how an anonymous request is processed.

Choosing this body threshold is an application design decision. The source supplies the value; it does not establish that this is the right threshold for every upload service.

The added branch sits before the reader wrapper and multipart parser. Excerpt from internal/handler/upload.go:

The decision uses the declared length before reading body bytes. Once that length exceeds the threshold, the handler already knows which response it intends to send. It does not parse the multipart form or inspect the image on this branch.

It still reads from the body before responding. Those bytes go to io.Discard; they are not accepted as an upload. The purpose, stated in the comments, is to let the 400 travel back through Apache while accommodating data the client has already sent.

The selected status is 400, with the existing file-too-large message. That is the application's response choice. The patch changes how the handler reaches that response rather than increasing the accepted upload size.

Multiplying the body threshold by five gives a discard cap of 25 MiB. That value is a separate design decision: the comments explicitly reject unbounded draining as a way for a client to make the server keep reading indefinitely.

The operation attempts to copy up to that amount from the body. The Go documentation for CopyN says it copies the requested count or stops on an error, returning the copied count and an error. This handler ignores both return values and proceeds to write 400.

For bodies whose actual size matches their declared size, a body over 5 MiB and no larger than 25 MiB fits within the drain budget. An earlier read error can still prevent a complete drain. A body larger than 25 MiB can leave bytes unread after the cap is reached.

Those consequences follow from the code. They do not establish that every oversized upload now avoids 502. The handler attempts a bounded accommodation of the proxy path; it does not verify that all bytes were consumed or guarantee delivery of its response.

A byte cap also should not be described as a time limit. This branch specifies an amount to discard, not a duration. Any claim about complete timeout protection would need evidence beyond these lines.

The declared length check is not the only protection. Requests that bypass it still encounter the original wrapper and parser. Excerpt from internal/handler/upload.go:

This includes requests without a declared length and those declaring a length at or below the threshold. The nearby comment also identifies an inaccurate declaration as a reason to retain the reader guard.

The branches therefore serve different purposes. Declared oversize selects the capped drain and rejection. Otherwise, actual reading remains bounded by MaxBytesReader before multipart parsing. Removing that wrapper would discard the protection for requests the length check cannot reject in advance.

There is another detail in the error handling: every error returned by this multipart parsing call maps to the same file-too-large message. Seeing that message is not, by itself, proof that the reader limit caused the parse error.

The history documents the earlier proxy failure. The current source contains the declared-length branch, the 25 MiB discard cap, and the retained 5 MiB reader limit. These are inspectable implementation facts.

The graphics README reports no regression test for the declared-length drain or Apache workaround in this checkout. Nearby image tests cover other concerns. They do not demonstrate that this response reaches a browser through Apache, and no such regression coverage is claimed here.

For a similar investigation, compare direct and proxied responses, then inspect what happens to unread request data when the handler rejects it. Keep the acceptance threshold, drain budget, and unknown-length behavior explicit. This patch makes those choices visible, while leaving a clear boundary around what its code and historical observation can support.

#9715. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. Hope you like this article if you have any question let me know in the comments section

#9713. How quarterly estimated tax actually works for freelance developers (with the math in JS)

Disclosure: I wrote this with help from an AI assistant. Every number below was computed by the code in this post and checked against the IRS worksheet. It's US federal only, for tax year 2026, and it isn't tax advice.

The first year you freelance, nobody withholds tax from your invoices. The IRS still expects the money during the year, not in April, and it charges a penalty if you wait. The rules behind that are spread across Form 1040-ES, Schedule SE, and Pub 505. Here's how they fit together, with code you can run.

You have to make estimated payments if both of these are true:

If you have a W-2 job too, its withholding counts. More on that below, because it's the most useful trick in this post.

The four payment periods for 2026 are uneven:

You can skip the January payment if you file your 2026 return by February 1, 2027 and pay the whole balance with it. If your income is lumpy (one big contract in the fall, say), the annualized income installment method (Form 2210, Schedule AI) lets you pay less in the early periods. Otherwise the IRS assumes you owed a quarter of the year's amount at each date.

Freelancers pay self-employment (SE) tax on top of income tax. SE tax is the employer and employee halves of Social Security and Medicare that a W-2 employer would split with you:

Then, for income tax, three things come off your profit before the brackets apply: half of your SE tax, the standard deduction ($16,100 single in 2026), and the qualified business income (QBI) deduction, which is 20% of your business income, capped at 20% of your taxable income.

This covers the common case: single filer, freelance profit only, under about $200k. It matches the full engine (linked at the end) to the cent on every profit from $0 to $195,000 in $7 steps, 27,858 cases.

That's about 21.5% of profit. Note that SE tax is almost twice the income tax here. People who only plan for "my tax bracket" underestimate badly.

Paying 90% of this year's tax means $4,346.09 each quarter. But you don't have to guess this year's number. That's the next part.

You avoid the underpayment penalty if your payments add up to the smaller of:

Say last year you owed $14,000 in total, with AGI under $150k. Pay $3,500 a quarter and you're safe from the penalty, even though this year's tax is $19,316. You'll owe the other $5,316 in April, with no penalty. If last year's AGI had been $160,000, the target is 110%: $15,400, or $3,850 a quarter.

For a growing freelance business this is the easiest plan: last year's number is known in advance, so you don't have to forecast. Just set aside the difference for April.

The penalty is figured per period: each underpayment for the number of days it stays unpaid. A big catch-up payment in December doesn't undo a short payment in April.

Withholding is different. Unless you elect otherwise, the IRS treats tax withheld from a paycheck as paid in four equal parts on the four due dates, no matter when it was actually withheld. Pub 505 puts it as "one-fourth of your estimated withholding is considered withheld on the due date of each payment period." So if you have a W-2 job plus side contracts, you can often skip estimated payments entirely: raise your withholding on Form W-4 (Step 4(c), "extra withholding") to cover the side income. That works even if you raise it in October.

Example: $120,000 salary plus $30,000 of side profit. Total 2026 tax: $27,125.93. If your paycheck withholding is $17,000 and last year's total tax was also $17,000, withholding already meets the 100% safe harbor, so no estimated payments are required. You'll still owe about $10,126 at filing time, so set it aside.

That example also shows the real cost of side income: the $30k adds about $9,556 of tax, 31.9 cents per dollar, because it lands in your top bracket and carries SE tax too.

IRS Direct Pay or your IRS online account (irs.gov/payments) is free. Choose "Estimated Tax" and "1040ES" with the right tax year. Keep the confirmation numbers. You'll enter the total on your return.

The code above is a cut-down version of an open-source engine I maintain. It also handles W-2 wages, married filing jointly and the other statuses, Additional Medicare Tax, the QBI phase-out, the safe harbor, and 2027 numbers. It has zero dependencies and is tested against hand-worked IRS worksheet examples. It runs from the terminal:

Sources: Form 1040-ES (2026), Rev. Proc. 2025-32, Pub 505. State tax is separate and not covered here. If you spot a mistake, open an issue on the repo and I'll fix it.

#9711. Can You Be Too Successful to Fire? Market Basket's Board Said No

Chief Strategy Officer | Board Dir. | AI | Org. & Ops. Effectiveness | Corp. Finance | Capital Markets | VC & PE | https://sanforddiday.com

Chief Strategy Officer | Board Dir. | AI | Org. & Ops. Effectiveness | Corp. Finance | Capital Markets | VC & PE | https://sanforddiday.com

Chief Strategy Officer | Board Dir. | AI | Org. & Ops. Effectiveness | Corp. Finance | Capital Markets | VC & PE | https://sanforddiday.com

Strong operating results did not settle Market Basket's boardroom fight. On April 20, 2026, Vice Chancellor J. Travis Laster of the Delaware Court of Chancery upheld the suspension and subsequent firing of longtime president and CEO Arthur T. Demoulas, while acknowledging the company's operating success (DSM HoldCo). The central question was whether the directors acted in good faith in exercising their authority, not whether firing Demoulas was the best business choice.

The ruling separates authority to remove a CEO from the wisdom of that decision. This article and this series draw a broader governance lesson from that distinction: a board's job is to protect the company's enduring character and accountability, not just referee its machinery. The three-day trial addressed the narrower question of whether these directors acted lawfully (Moran; DSM HoldCo).

The business judgment rule limits judicial second-guessing when it applies. In this case, Demoulas had to prove that a majority of the directors acted in bad faith. The court found that he failed to do so (DSM HoldCo). Laster took the case under submission on February 25, 2026, and issued his opinion on April 20. The outcome established that Demoulas had not met that burden, rather than that the board had chosen wisely. Honesty alone does not capture the rule's full requirements.

Market Basket's public story centers on low prices and loyal cashiers. In 2014, workers shut down stores for weeks to demand Demoulas's reinstatement after an earlier ouster by his cousins. The walkout made the chain a folk-hero story and ended in a $1.6 billion buyout that put Demoulas and his three sisters in sole control of the company (Chesto). Eleven years later, the boardroom fight pitted him against the sisters who had once helped bring him back. That history explains the public stakes; customer loyalty alone did not resolve the legal question.

Demoulas grew Market Basket into an operation generating roughly $8 billion in annual revenue and employing more than 30,000 people (Chesto). By any ordinary measure, he did his job well, and the court did not dispute that. Laster wrote that Demoulas "proved to be an excellent operator, but an imperious leader," adding that strong performance is "not the only dimension of a CEO's job" (DSM HoldCo).

The board's concerns extended beyond operating results. In August 2024, it gave Demoulas a five-item "Issues List" covering budgets, capital expenditure approvals, and succession, including rejecting automatic succession by his children. The opinion describes his failure to resolve those issues (DSM HoldCo). Reports of a possible walkout and boycott heightened the directors' concerns in spring 2025. They suspended him in May pending an outside investigation by Quinn Emanuel, then terminated him in September after unsuccessful mediation (DSM HoldCo; Solis). The investigation's conclusions supported the board's position. Those investigative conclusions and the court's findings represent separate parts of the record.

Two companies, DSM HoldCo and Demoulas Super Markets, brought the Section 225 action with directors Jay Hachigian, Steven Collins, and Michael Keyes to confirm the validity of Demoulas's removal. Demoulas counterclaimed that the directors breached their fiduciary duties by suspending and terminating him. He sought reinstatement as president and CEO (DSM HoldCo; Pelletiere and Boston 25 News Staff). At trial, he had to prove that a majority of the directors had acted in bad faith. He did not meet that burden. Laster rejected the claim that the directors were beholden to the sisters and found a rational basis for their concern about a repeat of 2014. The court upheld the removal (DSM HoldCo).

This case turns on a distinction between operating performance and governance cooperation, rather than a single verdict on a CEO. The two dimensions ask different questions. Collapsing them into one obscures what the court decided.

Operating performance covers revenue, growth, and customer loyalty, familiar subjects in shareholder letters. Governance cooperation asks different questions: whether management gives directors transparent information, plans succession honestly, and accepts that a board's authority to ask questions does not shrink as the business grows. Strong results and legitimate oversight address distinct responsibilities; neither cancels the other. The board, in turn, must exercise its authority for the company, not merely demand obedience.

Could the directors act independently of a powerful executive and obtain the information they needed to govern? Those are the two questions in the series' Independence and Information framework. In this dispute, their documentation began with unresolved issues in 2024 and continued through the May 2025 suspension pending investigation, the investigation itself, and unsuccessful mediation before termination. The court upheld their exercise of judgment on that record (DSM HoldCo). The documents supported the decision as evidence; the obligation to act in the company's interests remained.

The independence question starts with the family dispute. Outside status alone cannot establish a director's independence. Selection by one side of the family, by contrast, does not by itself prove bad faith. What matters is whether the directors exercised judgment for the company rather than serving a faction. The court rejected Demoulas's challenge on the record before it (DSM HoldCo).

None of this settles what Market Basket's culture or legacy required. Demoulas led a business with substantial employee and customer loyalty, and his supporters argue that the hands-on style they associate with "Artie T." helped sustain that success across roughly ninety stores. A spokesperson for Demoulas acknowledged that Delaware's deference to directors imposed high hurdles, but pointed to strong performance as evidence the company did not need fixing (Pelletiere and Boston 25 News Staff). That argument deserves a hearing. It is not a frivolous one.

The strongest objection concerns what removal would mean for the business. The directors could have authority to act without proving that firing Demoulas would preserve Market Basket's advantages better than a workable compromise. Strong results, meanwhile, could not put the CEO beyond oversight. The ruling resolves the legal challenge. It cannot show how the company would have fared under a different arrangement.

The unresolved business question leaves responsibilities intact on both sides. Strong operating results do not erase a board's oversight role. The board must exercise authority over management for the company, rather than treat control as an end in itself. Successful operations and legitimate oversight must coexist.

Section 225 supplied a focused procedure for determining whether Demoulas's removal was valid. The case moved from the September 2025 filing to the April 20, 2026 post-trial opinion in about seven months (DSM HoldCo; Vinson & Elkins). That pace gave this particular leadership dispute a prompt answer. The record also extended beyond the termination meeting: unresolved governance requests, an outside investigation, and unsuccessful mediation preceded the firing.

Ten days after the ruling, Market Basket named a former teenage bagger as its new president. Chuck Casassa, the operations director, joined the chain at fourteen in 1976. The April 30, 2026 announcement also marked the retirement of interim CEO Don Mulligan after more than four decades with the company, including 27 years as CFO (Riley). Separately, the board said the company was not for sale, would remain family-owned, and expected to work productively with Demoulas as a shareholder (Pelletiere and Boston 25 News Staff). Those statements describe the board's intentions. The long-term effects of its decision remain an open question.

The ruling gives family-company executives a clear answer to a recurring governance question: strong operating results do not put management beyond legitimate oversight. Performance is part of the job, not the whole job. Accountability matters too. Directors have a corresponding responsibility to exercise their authority on behalf of the company.

#9706. Jensen Huang Affair Timeline: Every Date, Interview and Megaspeed Mention From 2024 to Now

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted on November 8, 2026 that he "was unfaithful to my wife," in an all-staff email Nvidia posted to its newsroom. The woman, per The New York Times as summarized by the SF Standard, is Alice Huang (Huang Le, no relation), a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of working for China's Ministry of State Security. No public record gives the affair's start date. The earliest documented meeting is a June 2024 Taipei bar night during Computex; TechCrunch reports they "reportedly met at an Nvidia event in early 2024."

The espionage claims come from unnamed U.S. officials. Alice Huang has not been charged or commented, China calls the claims a "smear," and Nvidia's board says it has "no reason to believe" secrets were compromised.

Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen based in Singapore who ran Megaspeed, the company that became Nvidia's biggest Southeast Asian customer. Most of her résumé cannot be independently verified.

Alice Huang; Huang Le; some Chinese reports render it Huang Xiaole

About 4 years as a reporter at Hunan TV and CCTV, then about 8 years in finance at HSBC private banking and CITIC Securities, per a Chinese fund-database profile

The New York Post found no reporter profile at either broadcaster; the NYT could not confirm her state-media or banking jobs

Executive director of a Shanghai fund (Shanghai Hexi Investment) that invested in 7Road

Managing director from March 2023; resigned as a director by Nov. 10, 2023; later called herself chief executive

Ties to Gigabyte leaders, Shanghai and Zhejiang data-center investors, and a cybersecurity unit of a Chinese military-tech developer

Not charged; no public comment; whereabouts unknown

Megaspeed was registered in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International and renamed in March 2023, the same month she joined, according to IBTimes. Its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, bought nearly $2 billion in Nvidia chips, mostly through the U.S. arm of entity-listed Inspur, the NYT reported. A Megaspeed-linked Malaysian company bought at least $4.8 billion in Nvidia equipment between June 2024 and February 2026, per OfficeChai's summary, and the Financial Times reported its balance sheet grew from $33 million to $3 billion in 2024. Megaspeed denies smuggling and has not been charged.

The affair's start date is not public. A U.S. memo reported by the Financial Times says officials do not know whether her alleged recruitment by Chinese intelligence came before or after the relationship began (OfficeChai's summary).

Nvidia published Jensen's Nov. 8, 2026 email on its own newsroom under the title "A Message to Our Company", alongside a separate "Statement From NVIDIA Board of Directors." The email never names Alice Huang and never mentions espionage directly; it refers only to "national security concerns raised in news reports."

The lines that matter, as quoted by Al Jazeera, Yahoo Finance and Business Standard:

The board's statement, per Tom's Hardware, puts "a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel" in charge and says it has "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised." Spokesperson John Rizzo added that "Today's news will not slow Nvidia" (SF Standard). Jensen has been married to Lori Huang for 41 years (Tom's Hardware).

Of 12 verified on-record interviews and press sessions since June 2024, Jensen discussed China in 11 and Megaspeed in exactly one: the late-October 2026 Bloomberg interview, after the NYT report. Jensen gives dozens of interviews a year, so this table covers the ones with a verifiable date and source, oldest first.

"There's no evidence of any AI chip diversion"

Export controls were "a failure"; one day before the Computex dinner

China International Supply Chain Expo, Beijing

H20 sales resuming; Huawei is "a formidable company"

"We went from 95% market share to 0%"; came four days after the NYT's first Megaspeed story

H200 approval may come quietly via purchase orders

"We have received purchase orders from many customers"

Two separate AI ecosystems are "not wise"

DeepSeek on Huawei chips is "a horrible outcome for our nation"

Dealings were "completely normal and not unusual"

Across 2025, Nvidia's comments on Megaspeed came only from spokespeople, never from Jensen on the record: John Rizzo to the NYT in October 2025 and the company to Bloomberg in December 2025.

Jensen has spoken about Megaspeed on the record once that we can find: a Bloomberg News interview after the Oct. 29, 2026 NYT report. Everything else came from Nvidia spokespeople or the board.

Megaspeed is "wholly owned and operated by a company based and headquartered outside China"; staff "found no evidence of diversion"; the Taipei bar night was routine

Megaspeed is "a cloud service permitted under the export control rules"; Nvidia asked Washington whether to cut it off and was told no

"The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year"

"Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual." Said she had left Megaspeed and the U.S. government never told him of its suspicions

Cloud partners "do not ask us to seek changes in US law or advocate for sales to China"

No Megaspeed mention; points only to "national security concerns raised in news reports"

Twelve days separate "completely normal" from "I was unfaithful to my wife," which is why Fortune reports the board's probe could examine Jensen's earlier statements.

Unproven: that Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset (unnamed officials' assessment, which Reuters "could not independently verify," per Tech Times); that she obtained Nvidia secrets; that Megaspeed diverted chips; and when the affair began. No public reporting shows Jensen knowingly passed information to anyone. As TechCrunch notes, his push for China access predates the 2024 meeting.

#9705. Secure Browser Direct Uploads: Object Storage API Selection Explained

Use a short-lived, restricted presigned upload URL when a fintech browser sends a large file directly to object storage. The backend authorizes one tenant and snapshot key, the browser sends the bytes to the returned URL, and the application records the result before it treats the snapshot as restorable.

Throughput is only the first filter. The provider also has to support a defensible restore record, predictable tenant boundaries, and a cleanup policy. A 50 GB backup that uploads quickly but cannot be proven immutable is a poor financial control. Infrai is an early candidate for the authorization leg when a plain REST request is preferable to adding a storage SDK; its single key and one bill can also reduce the credential and reconciliation work required for the rest of the backend process. Those are integration conveniences, not substitutes for retention or immutability controls.

Start with the restore, not the upload button. A selected snapshot should have a database record containing its tenant, object key, creation state, and final verification state. The storage object is evidence in that record, not the record itself.

The browser should receive a URL scoped to one target object and limited in time. An expired URL must fail. A URL for tenant 41 must not be usable for tenant 42. The server should never forward the file bytes merely because it is easier to inspect an HTTP stream there.

There is an important negative test: two writers target the same snapshot key. This storage model has no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrent-write exclusion needs a queue or database coordinator. Consumer and retry logic must be idempotent; otherwise a timeout can leave two business records pointing at an ambiguous object. Consider a restore operator selecting tenant-42/snapshot-2026-10-23.dump while a second job retries after a lost response: the object name alone does not tell the operator whether the first job committed, whether the second job overwrote it, or whether the manifest is stale. The coordinator has to make that state explicit, and the post-upload verification has to be tied to the same snapshot identity. This is the uncomfortable test.

The immutability question is separate. There is no object versioning or object lock, so a financial archive that requires WORM behavior needs an external control or a storage specialist. There is no public-read ACL or permanent public URL either. That rules out static-site assets, permanent public links, and image-hosting use cases.

Amazon S3 is the reference point when versioning, object lock, lifecycle controls, multipart tooling, and cross-region patterns are mandatory. Its ecosystem is a strength for regulated archives, while its IAM policy and credential surface add material audit work.

Supabase Storage fits an application whose authentication, database records, and storage policies already live in Supabase. The integration can be attractive for that existing shape, but the team still has to verify that its policy and retention behavior produce the tenant isolation and restore evidence the ledger requires.

Cloudflare R2 is a useful comparison for object-heavy web workloads that value an S3-compatible interface alongside the Cloudflare edge. It is a specialist storage choice; versioning, retention, restore authorization, and reconciliation remain design responsibilities.

Infrai is worth testing when the required boundary is a plain REST call with no storage SDK to install or version. The discovery surface is public and self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, which makes a small cross-language evaluation easier to reproduce. The live platform covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key.

The second advantage is breadth rather than transport: 295 routes across 20 modules are available under one key. Infrai offers one key for everything and one bill across that backend capability surface. For a process that couples snapshot authorization with other backend work, this removes the concrete friction of collecting another credential and reconciling another account. It does not remove the need to audit concentrated trust.

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the presign leg when SDK-free integration and a shared backend credential matter more than storage-specialist controls, and provide CORS, retention, and immutability elsewhere. Choose S3 when object lock or replication is mandatory, Supabase when its existing policy and data integration remove meaningful work, and R2 when its object-storage operating model is the better fit.

Infrai also has no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool, and the stated vendor coverage does not include GCS or B2. That is the boundary a fair comparison must keep visible.

The dominant transfer term is the file itself. A 50 GB tenant export sent through an application server crosses that server's network boundary before reaching object storage; a selected restore crosses another boundary on its way to an operator or recovery job. The application must hold connections, enforce timeouts, and handle a client disappearing at 73 percent.

Direct upload changes that path. The backend makes a small authorization request, while the browser sends the bytes to storage. Storage and retrieval still exist as costs, and retention is still a governance decision. The change worth measuring is removal of the backend from the bulk data path.

Retention is where a fast upload can create a slow audit problem. Keeping every intermediate export makes an investigation easier but preserves more sensitive data. Deleting aggressively reduces retained data and increases the cost of reconstructing a point in time. A durable snapshot manifest should therefore live in the database, with the object key and verification state tied to it.

The practical sacrifice is failed multipart debris. Lifecycle retention is no shorter than 1 day, and there is no automatic rule for cleaning up multipart fragments. A team that deletes such material sooner must own that cleanup outside the storage lifecycle; a team that keeps it longer accepts extra sensitive data and an additional audit surface.

Use identical inputs for every candidate: a 1 GB file, a 50 GB file, an interrupted upload, a duplicate retry, an expired URL, and two writers targeting the same snapshot key. Record backend bytes transferred, upload completion, rejection of the expired URL, retained objects after cleanup, and whether the restore manifest identifies exactly one object and tenant.

For the REST presign leg, the request shape is one explicit POST to the storage object presign operation. The returned URL is a separate destination: do not send the platform bearer credential to it.

Pass the direct-upload design only if the application server never receives file bytes, an expired or wrong-scope URL is rejected, a retry produces one auditable snapshot identity, and a failed transfer leaves no ungoverned object after the chosen cleanup window. If the archive must be immutable, require object lock or an external WORM control that the evidence can verify.

The decision rule is simple: select the least complex option that passes those tests for the largest file class actually present. The smallest implementation is not automatically the smallest control burden.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the storage presign documentation and verify the response handoff before exposing it to a browser.

#9703. Proxy dân cư tĩnh (ISP): khi nào nên thuê IP cố định thay vì xoay?

Posted on Nov 10 • Originally published at viblo.asia

Hướng dẫn chọn IP cố định: whitelist với đối tác, tài khoản được phép quản lý, QA bản địa hoá, checkout, và thuê theo IP/tháng hay trả theo GB.

Công khai: Mình đang làm việc tại ipvora, một dịch vụ residential proxy. Toàn bộ code trong bài là code chung, chạy được với bất kỳ nhà cung cấp nào hỗ trợ HTTP/HTTPS/SOCKS5.

Proxy xoay phù hợp với thu thập dữ liệu công khai hay nghiên cứu thị trường: mỗi request có thể ra IP khác. Nhưng một số việc sẽ hỏng nếu IP thay đổi — đối tác chỉ nhận địa chỉ đã khai báo, tài khoản bạn được phép quản lý cần ổn định nhiều ngày, QA bản địa hoá chạy suốt sprint, hoặc cổng thanh toán xem việc đổi IP như tín hiệu bất thường.

Bài này trả lời: khi nào nên thuê proxy dân cư tĩnh (static residential / ISP proxy), tức một IP cố định, thay vì xoay? Mình so sánh rotating, sticky session và static, nêu khác biệt cách tính phí, rồi đưa ví dụ Python (requests và tuỳ chọn httpx) dùng biến môi trường.

Datacenter proxy (IP trung tâm dữ liệu) nhanh và thường rẻ hơn, nhưng nhiều website nhận ra đây là IP máy chủ nên nội dung có thể khác người dùng dân dụng.

Nhiều đối tác B2B — cổng thanh toán, API ngân hàng hoặc ví điện tử, nền tảng quảng cáo, hệ thống kho — chỉ nhận kết nối từ IP đã khai báo (whitelist). Rotating buộc bạn nhờ đối tác cập nhật mỗi lần IP đổi; sticky hết hạn sau cửa sổ phiên, trong khi duyệt whitelist thường mất hàng ngày. Với proxy tĩnh, bạn gửi một lần địa chỉ rồi giữ nguyên nhiều tuần.

Gian hàng thương mại điện tử, tài khoản quảng cáo hay trang mạng xã hội của khách hàng thường theo dõi độ ổn định của IP. Cùng một tài khoản xuất hiện từ nhiều quốc gia, hoặc đổi IP liên tục trong ngày, có thể bị xem là chia sẻ tài khoản hay đăng nhập bất thường. Chỉ quản lý tài khoản bạn được phép quản lý — tài khoản công ty, khách đã ủy quyền, hoặc tài khoản thử nghiệm do đội ngũ bạn tạo.

Nhiều cổng thanh toán xem IP đổi giữa các bước (xem giỏ → điền địa chỉ → chọn phương thức → xác nhận) như tín hiệu gian lận, và có thể đối chiếu IP khi người dùng mở lại đơn vào ngày hôm sau. Sticky đủ cho một lần thanh toán trong cửa sổ phiên; nếu QA tạm dừng rồi chạy lại ngày mai, bạn cần IP cố định. Chỉ chạy trên staging, sandbox, hoặc production khi chủ hệ thống đã đồng ý — không dùng proxy để che vị trí nhằm vượt kiểm soát chống gian lận mà bạn không được phép kiểm thử.

Sticky không phải sản phẩm tách riêng, mà là cách dùng proxy xoay khi cần IP ổn định trong thời gian ngắn. Nếu nhu cầu đã vượt cửa sổ phiên, hãy thuê IP cố định thay vì cố kéo dài sticky.

Proxy xoay tính theo từng GB, hợp khi lưu lượng biến động và bạn cần nhiều IP. Proxy tĩnh trả mức cố định mỗi IP mỗi tháng; với ipvora, lưu lượng không giới hạn trong kỳ thuê. Nếu một IP phải bật cả ngày cho QA, hoặc vài người cùng dùng địa chỉ đã whitelist, tính theo tháng thường dễ dự toán hơn cộng từng GB.

Để dễ hình dung sự khác biệt, mình lấy bảng giá công khai của proxy dân cư tĩnh dành cho khách hàng Việt Nam làm mốc tham chiếu — nhà cung cấp khác sẽ có mức giá riêng, nhưng mô hình tính phí thường tương tự.

Với ipvora, proxy dân cư xoay tính phí theo dung lượng, gồm 10 gói từ 1 GB đến 5 TB: gói 1 GB giá $2.09 (thời hạn 30 ngày), gói 5 TB còn $1.39/GB. Từ các gói 100 GB trở lên, dung lượng còn lại không hết hạn. Thời gian giữ phiên (sticky) là 1–120 phút. Proxy dân cư tĩnh thuê theo tháng, khởi điểm từ $3.18/IP/tháng (một số khu vực có giá khác, ví dụ Hà Lan $4.88/IP/tháng), 5 Mbps mỗi IP và không giới hạn lưu lượng trong thời hạn thuê.

Chọn nhanh: nhiều trang độc lập, lưu lượng khó đoán → xoay, trả theo GB; luồng 15–90 phút cần cùng IP → sticky trên gói xoay; một hoặc vài IP phải giữ hàng tuần hay gắn whitelist → tĩnh, thuê theo IP/tháng.

Cả proxy xoay và proxy tĩnh của ipvora đều hỗ trợ HTTP, HTTPS và SOCKS5. Cách xác thực — user/password trong URL, cổng riêng, hay whitelist IP máy bạn — khác nhau giữa từng dashboard. Đừng đoán hostname hay cú pháp gateway; hãy lấy đúng giá trị từ trang quản trị bạn đang dùng.

Các ví dụ dưới đây chỉ dùng placeholder PROXY_HOST, PROXY_PORT, PROXY_USER, PROXY_PASS từ biến môi trường. Với SOCKS5 trong requests, nên dùng scheme socks5h:// để DNS phân giải phía proxy (quan trọng khi kiểm thử theo vùng). Ký tự đặc biệt trong mật khẩu (@, :, #, …) cần urllib.parse.quote(..., safe="") trước khi ghép URL.

Trước khi gửi địa chỉ cho đối tác whitelist hoặc gắn vào bộ QA nhiều ngày, hãy kiểm tra IP không đổi qua nhiều lần gọi.

requests[socks] cài PySocks để hiểu URL socks5h://; httpx[socks] cài socksio nếu dùng SOCKS5 với httpx.

Nếu script báo IP đã đổi, đừng gửi địa chỉ đó cho đối tác: có thể bạn đang trỏ nhầm endpoint xoay hoặc lấy sai thông tin từ dashboard.

Muốn dùng SOCKS5 với httpx, đổi scheme trong proxy_url() thành socks5:// (cần đã cài httpx[socks]).

Thuê IP cố định không thay đổi nghĩa vụ khi bạn gửi request nhân danh mình:

#9702. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9700. 5 Open-Source & Free Projects for Coffee Lovers — To Support Via Kivach

If you can’t live without a sacred cup of coffee in the morning or even if you work directly in the industry at a professional level, you may want to know that there are many open-source projects in the field. From brewing timers and roast profiling to apps that help you find great cafés, developers are creating useful tools that coffee lovers can enjoy for free.

Given that these projects are open-source, you can check their code, explore how they work, or help improve them yourself. The community is in charge, and funding also comes from the community itself. That’s why, if one of the projects below becomes one of your favorites, you can support it with Kivach. This is an Obyte-based crypto donation platform where you can send some funds to any GitHub project you want.

Now, let’s discover some interesting coffee-centered apps.

Created by Lars Saalbach back in 2017, Beanconqueror has grown into a full coffee-tracking platform for Android and iOS. Its first application version appeared that year, followed by redesigns and integrations with Bluetooth scales, pressure sensors, and espresso equipment.

The app promises to be “Everything You Need for Brewing Perfection.” You can record beans, grinders, brewing methods, grind size, dose, brewing time, first drip, water recipes, tasting notes, and ratings. It also supports V60, AeroPress, espresso, Orea, and other preparation methods, plus live graphs from compatible Bluetooth scales and pressure devices.

Like any other app in this list, it's free, and anyone can contribute via GitHub. You can also offer suggestions and ask for compatibility with new devices. As for funding, Saalbach accepts one-time or recurring support and GitHub sponsorships, giving users several ways to help keep the project going. You can send him crypto tips via Kivach, too.

This one is more of a step-by-step style. Released in 2023 by Anton Karliner, Timer.Coffee will guide you through the preparation of different types of brews, with several methods and ingredients. As the name suggests, it includes a timer for every step, but there are more features to explore on iOS, Android, and its web app.

You can find over 40 brewing recipes with at least 20 methods and variations here, a coffee-and-water calculator, custom grind settings, a favorites section, a brew diary, bean management, step alerts, device synchronization, and recipe sharing. There’s also a live view of what other users are brewing, and the app can keep the timer running even if the phone is locked. All of this is available in 22 languages.

Timer.Coffee is user-friendly and open to everyone. As such, anyone can contribute, either with code and translations or new recipes and suggestions. If you want to support the author directly, you can donate some crypto funds through Kivach.

Especially designed for coffee roasters, Artisan Scope was released in 2009 by Marko Luther and Rafael Cobo. It was initially a simple program to control coffee roasting temperature, but over the years it’s become a complete platform for creating roasting profiles, automation, and monitoring for individual and commercial use.

Artisan records, analyzes, and can control roast profiles when connected to suitable thermocouples, data loggers, PID controllers, and roasting machines. It offers support for 50+ devices and 80+ brands, a flexible interface in 30+ languages, automated reproduction of roasts, profile design, and spider charts. Additionally, it has tools for energy and CO2 tracking, reporting, inventory management, and production planning.

You can use it at any time for free, but there’s also a premium version with some extra features —particularly for companies. The software is available on GitHub, and any kind of contribution is welcome. Their funding mostly comes from community donations, which are encouraged. To send some crypto to this project, you can use Kivach.

In case you’re not exactly a professional in the industry, there are, of course, some more lighthearted options. Like this little game. Initially "attempted" by Shamus Peveril and Gavin Anderegg in 2011, Coffee Quest ended up being released by them and Chris Whalen in 2014 as part of the MindSea Hackathon. Now, you can enjoy it as a web app about business and caffeine.

The controls are extremely easy: only the direction arrows (down, up, left, right). This way, you’ll guide a businessman who needs more caffeine to keep moving forward while earning interest from banks, making sales, paying taxes, and discovering new cafes. The challenge is to not run out of caffeine (energy) while earning or even losing some money. Each new level creates a fresh 12×12 map, and the game continues until the player's caffeine runs out.

Besides the web app, Coffee Quest is available on GitHub for developers to contribute code. This is an indie project, so funding comes entirely from the authors. Crypto donations are possible via Kivach.

As the author put it, this is “a coffee shop map that isn't Google; community vetted spots only.” Created by Poorva Nangia in 2026, this app is barely starting to help users find specialty coffee shops in a few cities. It uses Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Mapbox GL, and Supabase, with a map interface for discovering a small set of real locations.

For now, you can enter this map on a web app and find community-added cafés in San Francisco (US) and the Indian cities Bombay, Delhi, and Gurgaon. Every place includes the name, rating with stars, address, coffee quality, if it’s work-friendly (WiFi, outlets, etc.), and if it’s comfortable to stay (seating and service). You can also add notes and likes or dislikes.

Users can request new cities and add new cafés, including the above data. There’s currently no listed funding method or donation program for Find My Coffee, so supporting the developer through contributions, feedback, or code may be the most direct route. To donate crypto, you can find this project on Kivach.

Donating to a GitHub project through Kivach takes just a few steps. Enter the repository name, select the network and token you want to use, specify the amount, and just confirm the donation. That’s it! You’ll need a funded crypto wallet, such as an Obyte wallet, and the developer must be notified so they can claim the contribution.

For maintainers, claiming a donation requires a free GitHub attestation with a chatbot in the Obyte wallet. This verification links the GitHub account to the person claiming the funds. After that, the donation can be collected in full or shared with other repositories, allowing maintainers to support projects they value too.
