#9699. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

The fastest way to troubleshoot is to check each layer in order instead of changing configuration randomly.

Troubleshooting rule: Fix cluster state before investigating client connectivity.

If the cluster components appear healthy, check whether the target service is listening.

Check the instance status and actual port configuration before changing anything.

Case 2: The port listens only on 127.0.0.1.

A local connection may work, but a remote client cannot access a service bound exclusively to the loopback interface.

Check the listening address as well as the port number.

For GBase Database(GBase 8c), the actual service port should be confirmed from the deployment configuration rather than assumed from an example.

If the port is listening and network connectivity is available, the next step is authentication and access control.

For PostgreSQL-compatible connection management in GBase Database, inspect pg_hba.conf in the relevant data directory.

This file defines which client addresses, users, and authentication methods are allowed to connect.

After modifying the file, reload the relevant database configuration using the supported procedure for your deployment.

Do not confuse authentication failures with connection refusal. They indicate different troubleshooting layers.

In a distributed GBase Database deployment, connect through the appropriate CN endpoint for normal application access.

Also distinguish primary and standby behavior. A standby may support read-only operations while rejecting writes, depending on its role and configuration.

A successful connection does not automatically mean every SQL operation is permitted.

Sometimes the actual problem appears before the connection attempt.

This is not a database connection failure. It usually indicates that the required environment variables or executable paths have not been loaded.

Alternatively, reconnect using the intended gbase account and verify the database environment.

Check that the executable path is available before continuing with connection troubleshooting.

#9693. Sleep Tech Needs to Prove More Than a Change in Brain Waves

Neuropsychologist,VR therapy innovator, and founder of X-Technology. Focused on AI/VR solutions for cancer & Alzheimer’s

Neuropsychologist,VR therapy innovator, and founder of X-Technology. Focused on AI/VR solutions for cancer & Alzheimer’s

Neuropsychologist,VR therapy innovator, and founder of X-Technology. Focused on AI/VR solutions for cancer & Alzheimer’s

An experiment can succeed while the question a customer cares about remains unanswered.

In a study published on 15 October 2026 in Sensors, researchers used a wireless EEG headband to time brief sounds to slow oscillations during sleep. They found increases in slow-wave activity, independently checked against simultaneous laboratory recordings. The system could both guide stimulation and detect a physiological response.

That is a useful engineering result. Whether someone will feel more restored after using such a device is a further question.

The study analyzed 16 healthy young adults from 26 initially recorded, after exclusions for signal quality and other criteria. It covered one laboratory night. Researchers manually enabled stimulation during deep sleep and paused it when other sleep stages, movement or arousals appeared. It was a feasibility study, with an inventor’s patent interest disclosed, rather than a demonstration of lasting benefit from unsupervised use at home.

For people building sleep technology, the distinction should shape the product from the beginning. A physiological response is one part of the evidence needed to make a promise about recovery.

My perspective as a psychologist and founder of X Technology begins with the person using the system. What becomes easier for them? Falling asleep? Staying asleep? Getting through the next day without disabling fatigue? Those are different goals, and a convincing product should be clear about which one it has tested.

Pink noise describes how sound energy is distributed across frequencies. It does not specify a treatment, a dose, or the state of the person listening.

The distinction becomes clearer in research published in Neuron in 2013. Investigators delivered sounds in synchrony with ongoing slow oscillations during sleep. They reported improvements in slow-oscillation activity and memory consolidation. Stimulation delivered out of phase did not produce the same effects.

Timing was part of what was tested. A continuous recording does not reproduce a system that measures an ongoing brain rhythm and delivers sound at selected moments within it.

When discussing an acoustic intervention, I would therefore keep its sound spectrum, intensity, timing, and duration together with the participant’s state. Removing those conditions leaves a much broader claim than the experiment can support.

For a product team, this means checking whether the cited research actually resembles the experience being sold. Shared vocabulary such as “pink noise” or “brain waves” is insufficient. The relevant comparison includes the sensing, delivery method, target population, and intended outcome.

I would separate product validation into three questions. Each can guide a different development decision.

Can the system measure what it claims to measure?

Comparison with an appropriate reference method, including unsuccessful recordings

Whether acting on that measurement helps the user

Does the intervention produce its intended response?

A suitable control condition and a clearly defined physiological outcome

Whether the response improves the problem the user wants solved

Outcomes matched to the promise, assessed over a relevant period, alongside tolerability.

Whether the benefit extends to other people, settings or durations

The third question needs particular care. “Better sleep” can refer to time taken to fall asleep, fewer awakenings, subjective restfulness or daytime functioning. A study can support one of these without answering all the others.

There is evidence that moves beyond changes in brain rhythms. A 2024 randomized crossover trial in Scientific Reports tested sound timed to alpha oscillations before sleep. Among 21 participants included in the analysis, weekly average EEG-measured sleep-onset time was approximately 10.5 minutes shorter during stimulation than during silent sham recording.

That is a more direct test of a particular user problem. Its interpretation still needs the surrounding facts: 100 people enrolled, many were excluded or withdrew, and only 21 entered the final analysis. The authors were employees of the company that sponsored the study. The comparison was also short, so it cannot establish enduring benefit for every person with difficulty sleeping.

The useful response to such evidence is to describe the finding precisely and identify the next uncertainty. Dismissing it would waste potentially valuable progress. Expanding it into a general promise of restorative sleep would obscure what remains unknown.

A development team should write down every task a researcher performs during testing: fitting equipment, checking a signal, deciding when an intervention can begin, noticing a problem and stopping it.

Then it should specify who or what performs each task in the product.

If software takes over a decision, that decision needs evaluation. If the user takes it over, the instructions and the effort required become part of the intervention. If nobody takes it over, the home experience contains an unresolved dependency.

Consider a hypothetical headband that loses reliable contact during the night. What should the system do with the next scheduled stimulus? How should it distinguish an uninterpretable recording from a night with no apparent benefit? What should it tell the user the following morning?

These decisions deserve attention before adding a more attractive dashboard. I would want uncertainty to remain visible throughout the process, including in the final report. A product should be able to say that it could not assess the night reliably.

Evaluation should also account for people who cannot comfortably use the device or obtain usable measurements. Reporting results from successful recordings is necessary, but a prospective user also needs to understand how often that success was achievable.

Imagine someone who receives an encouraging sleep score but still wakes feeling exhausted. A useful interface should allow them to record that experience without implying that their perception is an error.

The opposite situation also deserves room: someone may feel better while a selected metric changes very little. The appropriate response is to investigate the disagreement and explain what the measurement can establish.

For product evaluation, I would pair the promised objective outcome with relevant reports of comfort, restfulness, and daytime function. I would also ask whether using the system creates additional bedtime effort. These are proposed design priorities, not findings established by the studies above.

The National Sleep Foundation’s 2026 position statement recognises the promise of consumer sleep technologies while emphasising the need to understand their utility and limitations. That is a productive starting point: make the technology useful, and make the boundaries understandable.

Before approving a claim such as “improves sleep,” I would ask a team to complete this sentence:

For these users, under these conditions, this version of the product improved this outcome over this period, compared with this alternative.

Any part of the evidence that cannot yet be filled in belongs in the development plan. Keeping those gaps visible allows a promising laboratory result to become a more credible product, with a promise the person using it can actually understand.

Agentic AI Should Not Become Your Emotional Operating System

#9692. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

#9688. Skip The Oil And Eggs: Add A Can Of Diet Coke To This Cake Mix For The Easiest Dessert

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Boxed cake mix is hard to beat when you need a dessert in a hurry, or if you just don't back your baking abilities. One of our favorites is Duncan Hines Devil's Food Cake, available on Amazon, which came in second in our boxed cake mix ranking. Like most packaged options, it comes with all the dry ingredients pre-measured, leaving you to add water, eggs, and vegetable oil. However, just because the instructions are printed on the back doesn't mean you have to follow them to the letter. In fact, you can swap all three for a can of Diet Coke and still come out with a soft, fluffy cake.

To understand why this works, it helps to know what eggs and oil actually do. Egg whites provide proteins that coagulate as the cake bakes, forming a structure that holds the batter together and helps trap the air responsible for its fluffy crumb. The fat from oil and egg yolks coats the flour particles and inhibits gluten development, helping produce a softer, more tender texture. Diet Coke also contributes to the cake's crumb and tenderness, but in a very different way.

Diet Coke's secret weapon is its carbonation. It contains dissolved carbon dioxide, which forms tiny bubbles when added to the batter. As the cake heats up in the oven, these bubbles expand and help the mixture rise. The soda's acidity can also react with leavening agents present in the mix, such as baking soda, further contributing to the cake's light texture. To top things off, a standard 12-ounce can of Diet Coke contains roughly the same volume as the combined water and oil that Duncan Hines' mix calls for, making it a super convenient add-in. If you don't have Diet Coke on hand, Coke Zero is a near-identical substitute.

To get the most out of this swap, start with a can of cold Diet Coke over one that's been sitting at room temperature. Ever noticed how a can of cold Diet Coke has that unbeatable crispness? That's because carbon dioxide prefers to hang around in cold liquids over warm ones. Once a soda can is cracked open, it releases gas, so a cold one retains its carbonation better as you prepare your batter. On that note, avoid over-mixing the batter as this can knock out the trapped gas. If you notice bubbling, that's a telling sign you need to slow down.

When swapping oil and eggs for Diet Coke, there's one important difference worth noting. Diet Coke famously contains no fat, so while it can help the cake rise, it can't replicate the richness that oil brings to the table. It's a great substitution if you're looking to make a lighter, less calorie-dense cake. But for something that'll produce a richer cake with all the same effects as Diet Coke, reach for good old full-sugar Coke instead.

Diet Coke gets its sweetness from aspartame, an artificial sweetener, which loses its sweetness when exposed to heat. Regular Coke opts for high-fructose corn syrup, which is essentially liquid sugar. Unlike aspartame, high fructose corn syrup thrives under heat, and is already a baking superstar. In the oven, its resident sugars caramelize to give the cake a richer flavor, gooier texture, and a beautifully browned color. In fact, any soda will work wonders for boxed cake mix; for a similarly rich flavor profile with a cherry backbone, pick up a can of Cherry Coke or Dr Pepper, or for something brighter, go for Sprite or 7UP.

#9686. Customers Have One Big Complaint About Costco's Bakery Items (Hint: It's Not Mold)

From Costco's bakery department come all the things that warm your heart, give you comfort, or enable you to celebrate your biggest life moments, like weddings or birthdays. Need an anniversary cake that feeds a crowd? Hosting a baby shower and want to make dozens of chicken salad sandwiches on flaky croissants? Or just want to bring home something a little special, like the luxurious year-round tuxedo cake, to treat yourself and your family? Costco can help you make that happen. Unfortunately, though, customers are noticing a troubling trend that doesn't involve molding or staling. According to their complaints, the warehouse's bakery items are gradually but distinctly suffering from a loss of quality.

On Reddit, one user remarked, "It's like they've forgotten what real, fresh bakery items are supposed to taste like," before going on to describe the muffins as resembling "cardboard soaked in artificial flavoring." Furthermore, while some folks praise the muffins' size, others blame shrinkflation for their frequent returns.

Another Redditor shared that the term "cloyingly sweet" is their "go-to description for almost anything in the bakery now." This is further reflected in a variety of comments stating that the bakery items just don't taste good anymore or don't have the same texture, with one Redditor calling them downright "awful."

It does seem like, these days, everything is getting worse and more expensive at the same time. And perhaps because of its sterling reputation as an employer and the fact that it hasn't thus far raised the price of its signature food court hot dog and soda combo, Costco seemed like it would be immune to those degradations.

However, a Costco bakery employee on Reddit described how, during their three-year tenure, the company gradually switched from scratch-made items to "frozen items that we would just toss in the oven." Another user who identified themselves as a Costco cake decorator shared that while "most items come in frozen," even the baked goods that do get made in-store tend to come from a mix. This contrasts with the account of yet another employee who claimed that when they worked there previously, many of the sweets and breads were indeed made from scratch, though they admitted that "things change fast."

Still, it seems the drop-off in quality is a matter of opinion, not fact. For example, one Reddit user wrote that their bakery "is still really good." Another user claimed theirs was "better than it has any right to be," with plenty of other commenters joining them in their praise.

#9683. Forget Mayo: Give Tuna Salad A Major Flavor Boost With This Bottled Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

If you're a fan of canned tuna and you get the right stuff, it can be perfectly tasty on a bed of lettuce — it's even one of the best foods to eat straight out of the can. It's a super high-protein food, and when you need a bit more flavor, a tuna salad is one of those simple meals that you can make quickly with just a little good mayo (our favorite being Kewpie) and mustard, maybe some pickle relish or diced cucumbers. That said, there are plenty of easy ways to take your plain tuna salad to the next level, but this is one you may have never thought of. You can skip the mayo completely and use a bottle of store-bought Caesar salad dressing in your next tuna salad. Our top pick for best Caesar salad dressing? Briannas Home Style Asiago Caesar Dressing, available at retailers like Walmart.

Using Caesar dressing in your tuna salad will highlight the salty, umami notes and give some nice vinegary undertones. Even bottled dressings typically have aged Italian cheeses, so they'll add amazing flavor that you can't get from most other off-the-shelf dressings. Plus, even though mayonnaise is often considered a tuna salad's best friend, when the salad is overly mixed (or even whipped with mayo), it can just turn out pasty and gooey and lose the texture of a perfectly good canned tuna altogether. With just a bit of Caesar dressing, mixed simply with a fork, you'll have a beautifully flavored tuna that's ready to add atop a bowl of greens or turn into a sandwich or a proper tuna melt.

Certainly not all Caesar dressings are created equal. Some may be a bit creamier or heavier on the garlic; some may contain anchovies, and some not. If you want more umami, go with something that has anchovies. And if you want the creamy factor that's closer to a traditional homemade tuna salad with mayo, you can often simply check for egg yolks or egg yolk powder on the ingredient list to get that extra hit of smooth, eggy flavor.

For the simplest Caesar tuna salad, per can of regular-sized tuna — which generally runs about five ounces (including the liquid) — you'll want about two and a half tablespoons of Caesar dressing. Whether you go with tuna in oil or in water is purely a personal choice. In oil, of course, the tuna will have more fat, so you may want to use less dressing. To add some crunch, diced onions, cukes, and celery are always a good idea, especially on a sandwich with a little cheese, lettuce, and tomato. Of course, you can add fresh or dried herbs and spices, like smoked paprika or even cayenne powder and hot sauce to add a little more intensity.

If you're making it to add to a full Caesar salad, you can simply toss canned tuna with some romaine lettuce, croutons, and Caesar dressing, then top with a little grated parmesan cheese. Caesar dressing also works great on baked salmon to keep it nice and moist. But when you're making your next simple tuna salad, you can maybe just go with a can of tuna and a few tablespoons of Caesar from the bottle, and you're good to go.

Despite its name, the classic French dip sandwich has distinctive ties to Los Angeles, California — the name is really just about the French bread it's served on. But unlike certain regional classics, like Indiana's giant pork tenderloin sandwich, the French dip has become an American standard that you can find at hundreds of eateries around the country. But which restaurant chain should you go to when you want a hit of that tasty beef and a dip of jus?

A separate Facebook user wrote that the sandwich was "pretty darn good," noting that the beef was well-prepared and fit perfectly on the bread, without the gristle that can sometimes ruin other sandwiches.

If you're not familiar with McAlister's Deli, the company operates over 580 locations in the U.S., from Florida to Pennsylvania and all across the South and Midwest. The restaurant's roast beef includes ingredients like vinegar, dried beef stock, and dehydrated onion and garlic, which presumably contribute to an extra-savory flavor. "This is very good," one YouTuber praised. "Very tender steak ... [and] melty cheese."

The sandwich itself comes with a free side, so you've already got a complete meal, but if you like to customize your order, you can add more depth with horseradish Dijon or yellow mustard to get it dialed in just how you like it. Additionally, those who want to recreate the experience at home can make some classic au jus to serve alongside their own roast beef sandwiches — you're going to want to combine the drippings with some red wine and herbs to get the flavor just right. But, well, if you don't want to go through the trouble, you can trust the Facebook user who called McAlister's sandwich "exceptionally flavorful" and enjoy it as-is. And, according to customers, you might just want to go with a signature sweet tea to wash it down.

#9673. Add This Spicy Ingredient To Ground Beef For A Burger That's 10x Juicier

If you're looking for a burger patty that not only has a bit of kick, but also plenty of juice, you need 'nduja, a legendary Italian sausage. It is not only extremely flavorful, but also quite high in fat and moisture, making it a perfect addition no matter how you like to cook your burgers.

'Nduja is technically a type of salami, except it's far more decadent and incorporates a hefty dose of Calabrian chili peppers for next-level taste. Its high fat-to-lean meat ratio makes it perfect for introducing more moisture, even in small amounts. Even if you only have exceptionally lean meat on hand, one part 'nduja to four parts beef keeps your patties tender and juicy, and even helps develop a better crust.

The idea is similar to many meatball recipes from around the world that incorporate both pork and beef. Whereas beef provides body and a hearty texture, pork can provide extra fat, flavor, and moisture, working together to cook up something truly delicious. The peppers also create a slightly savory and spicy flavor profile that, while immediately noticeable, isn't so overwhelming that you might need to change up your preferred toppings. Each bite will drip with flavorful juices that mix with your condiments for the most moisture-rich burger possible.

Incorporating anything into a burger is a bit of a tightrope walk. You want to disperse your ingredients evenly but not work the muscle fibers so much that your patties end up dense or tough. 'Nduja's texture makes this quite easy, but you'll want to be careful about what type of meat you add it to.

Since it has a spreadable, pâté-like texture, working 'nduja directly into the meat is quite easy. Whether you mix it in thoroughly or squeeze pinches into already formed patties for pockets of flavor, you get plenty of fatty juices. Still, if you're worried about overworking your patties or want to add the salty meat at the very last minute, 'nduja is typically safe to eat right out of the package. Treat it like cheese and add a dollop after flipping your patties, letting it melt over the whole thing for a juicy entree.

If you want a custom burger blend, you have to be mindful of the proper fat-to-meat ratio. 'Nduja's exceptional fat content means it's best to add it to already lean blends so you don't end up with anything too greasy. The leaner your beef, the more 'nduja you can incorporate, so it's a balance between how much of its flavor you want included. Something that's at least 85% lean is ideal, letting you incorporate enough to taste without adding so much that you can't appreciate the beef's natural flavor.

#9671. TikToker Makes French Onion Soup In The Microwave (We Tried It, It's Legit)

French onion soup is a classic dish that has roots in ancient Roman cuisine and was further developed in France throughout the 1700s. The version we know today has ties to the city of Lyon, but it didn't get its signature toppings of toasted bread and melted cheese until it became popular in Paris. It has since become a bistro favorite and a fixture on American tables. The only problem with the soup is that even a simple recipe requires a lot of time just to caramelize the onions to perfection — around 30 minutes, at least — and one quicker alternative resorts to using a packet of instant soup mix. A TikToker, however, found a middle path that takes around 15 minutes to prepare in total.

Microwaves are efficient at heating liquids, and since raw onions contain almost 90% water, this kitchen appliance can cook them in a fraction of the time it would take on a stovetop. Starting the process in a covered bowl will sweat the onions and conserve their juices while they soften. Finishing the cooking process uncovered then evaporates those juices and allows the onions to brown.

Using beef broth or stock is also one of the best ways to add flavor to this recipe, and heating everything together for a couple of minutes melds the flavors of all the ingredients into a harmonious soup. The use of croutons is also a genius tip that cuts back on the time it would take to slice and toast a baguette. While this recipe looks legit, it almost seems too good to be true, so I decided to test it out for myself.

The beautiful thing about this recipe is that it calls for ingredients you may already have in your kitchen, and when I realized that I didn't have to make a special trip to the supermarket, I knew I had to try it out for myself. I started by slicing half an onion — we recommend using a yellow onion for the best results. Microwaving it covered for three minutes gave me the same results as in the TikTok video. However, things took a turn when I proceeded to cook the onions uncovered.

The TikToker microwaved their onions for two increments of three minutes and 30 seconds and achieved a light caramelization. My onions already reached that level of browning after the first increment of cooking, and after another minute and a half, they began to burn. Since microwave strengths vary, I recommend cooking your onions in much shorter increments to prevent the same unpleasant results. If you really want to cut back on the time and are worried about burning your onions, opt for birista, or South Asian-style crispy fried onions, that don't require cooking.

The other elements of this recipe worked beautifully, though. The addition of Worcestershire sauce added some acidity and umami to balance the deep flavors of the onions. While half a teaspoon of garlic powder may seem like a lot to add to such a small quantity of soup, it actually played well with the onions and added an additional layer of flavor to the mix. The croutons also soaked up the broth without disintegrating into the soup. I used shredded Gruyère cheese for a traditional touch, which added more dimension to the soup, but mozzarella would also work well in this recipe.

#9666. Meatloaf Is So Much Juicier When You Add This Boxed Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When you want a meal that sticks to your ribs and brings a measure of comfort with every bite, you want a good, homemade meatloaf, one of America's favorite dinners. It's traditionally made with ground beef, though to keep things tender, people often include ground pork or Italian sausage. Some include a cooked-down vegetable mix to help the loaf stay moist, while others employ the use of milk. But there's a boxed (or bagged) ingredient likely already in your pantry that you might bring out next time you make meatloaf and want to avoid a crumbly, cracking mess, and it'll help create the juiciest version you've likely ever had. Instant mashed potatoes, which are great to keep on hand for soups and sauces, are about to be your secret weapon in the battle against dry meatloaf, too.

Instant mashed potatoes might sound like a strange mix-in, but hear us out. They're dehydrated and flaky, which makes them ideal when used in meatloaf because when those flakes get dampened by your other ingredients (meat, milk, egg), they thicken, adding bulk and binding the mixture together. More importantly, though, these hard-working flakes hold onto moisture, locking it inside the loaf inside instead of letting the juices run out quite so freely, so your dinner won't dry out during its long cook in the oven.

While moist meatloaf is reason enough to add instant mashed potatoes to the mix, there are a few other benefits worth considering. First and foremost: They're cheap, and they keep for a long time. You can typically get a box from Walmart for less than $4 (prices may vary), and its bags often start at just a buck apiece. Many brands can last up to a year, so you can keep them in your pantry, and they'll likely be good to go the next time you're in the mood for meatloaf (or shortcut gnocchi, for that matter).

Furthermore, most instant mashed potatoes are gluten-free. While you'll want to be sure to check the labels before using them, these potato flakes can often make meatloaf accessible to our friends and family with celiac disease or gluten sensitivities, since they can substitute for breadcrumbs.

Finally, a few tips when employing instant spuds in your dinner loaf. You might let them sit for a few minutes after combining them with the other ingredients, before you introduce the meat; this gives them the opportunity to "set up." And you're not confined to just plain buttery instant mashed potatoes. Give your supper a major upgrade with different flavors of boxed flakes, like sour cream and chives, four cheese, and more.

#9665. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

Cover photo and food styling by Liz Neily.

#9661. Not Butter Or Cheese: The Creamy Ingredient That Makes Grilled Cheese 10x Richer

Grilled cheese is already a decadent meal that requires little effort, but a different form of richness from meat, rather than cheese, can make it more complexly delicious. If you're going to reach for rich meat, then look no further than pâté, something that comes in enough variety to suit any cheese combination you choose for your sandwich.

Many of us are familiar with pâté on a charcuterie board, served with a light cracker so you can experience its full flavors. But it's a common sandwich ingredient — take, for example, French influence in the Vietnamese bánh mì, creating an international grilled cheese style that's as unique as it is delicious. As it heats, the pâté practically melts like a meaty butter, infusing your cheese and bread with all that richness and delivering a truly powerful taste. When done properly, the pâté should mix directly into the gooey cheese, creating a single filling with the best possible texture.

Thanks to its high fat content, pâté has a signature silky texture that's hard to find elsewhere. Even vegetarian varieties made from mushrooms, soft cheese like ricotta, and butter can be a spot of decadence on an otherwise straightforward meal. It has a remarkable capacity for taking even the most underrated cheeses and turning them into gooey perfection, even if they don't have much moisture or fat to begin with. Combined with a sturdy bread toasted with butter or mayo, each layer of your grilled cheese will end up impossibly rich.

Pâté is an extraordinarily delicate ingredient, so adding it to any hot recipe takes a bit of know-how. Some are designed to be eaten hot or cold, so selecting the right variety and application can prevent you from losing out on any of its delicious virtues. For example, a terrine — not to be confused with true pâté or even rillettes — warms beautifully.

Heating up a pâté made to be eaten cold may make it greasy and fall apart, rather than melt. Instead of these, look for ones used in pâté en croûte, a type of fluffy pastry that uses it as a filling. Just like a country variety, aka terrine, it has a coarser texture that adds a satisfying bite to your sandwich and won't split once heated. These can also come in a dizzying variety, from meaty ones seasoned with nothing but salt to ones laden with chopped vegetables, nuts, and spices.

A simple smear on one side of your bread does the trick just fine, and the direct contact with the bread lets it soak up excess fat as it heats. But if you use an aged or low-fat cheese, try incorporating it with another simple trick for a meltier result: grating the cheese first. By tossing the cheese with your pâté, you coat each individual strand with a bit of the fat and ensure that, when they melt, the two ingredients fuse together. If you use slices, it can also help to smear a bit of pâté on each one before layering them between your bread.

#9659. Grab This Packet Of Seasoning To Transform Store-Bought Snacks Into A Delicious Masterpiece

Many kitchens contain a well-stocked, if not cluttered, spice cabinet, making it easy to grab what you need when a recipe calls for spices. However, don't rule out using those jarred seasonings with store-bought snacks, too — taco seasoning is one such ideal candidate.

This savory spice blend is one of the kitchen's most versatile, useful in everything from elevating your grilled burgers to giving chicken tenders a delicious twist. Bringing together flavors like earthy ground cumin, sweet paprika, onion and chili powders, oregano, salt, and more, it's a testament to the idea that a good spice blend is greater than the sum of its parts. All the more reason to throw it on your favorite snack. Think the crunchy classics: Chex Mix, fresh or bagged popcorn, pretzels, a nut mix, or good ol' chips.

To make sure the seasoning sticks, you'll want to apply some heat and fat, not just sprinkle on the spices. Fold a packet into some tasty melted butter or coconut oil, then mix it into your snack of choice. Bake at around 350 degrees Fahrenheit, stirring occasionally, until you have a delectably browned and seasoned snack mix.

Seasonings are made for modifications. So if a simple dusting of taco seasoning isn't what you're craving, it's easy to fine-tune the flavors to your liking. An easy starting point is a sweet element — honey, agave syrup, or even maple syrup all pair fabulously with taco seasoning. Simply mix the sugary ingredient into the fat to lend the spiced mix an added dimension.

Alternatively, customize the flavors by mixing up the spice blend yourself. Taco seasoning can contain a variety of ingredients in numerous styles, so brighten up your snack seasoning with grated lime zest, or turn up the heat with cayenne or ground árbol chilies. Consider even amplifying the warmth with cinnamon or allspice — ingredients that'll pair terrifically with sweet flavors.

Alongside such reworked blends, keep expanding your store-bought snack repertoire. Throw in a bag of dry-roasted edamame beans, some Fritos, or plantain chips, or buy some chicharrones (fried pork rinds). Mix and match nibbles to your liking, dust with taco seasoning, then enjoy a new world of snackable possibilities.

#9654. Forget The McDonald's Egg McMuffin: The Spicier Option With Meaty Flavor

McDonald's Egg McMuffin helped put the chain's breakfast on the map, and while it remains one of the fast food joint's biggest sellers, it has since been joined by a pretty terrific supporting cast of fellow menu items. For example, the (surprisingly unseasoned) hash browns are a crispy and craveable addition to the lineup. But while the Egg McMuffin can certainly be meat-heavy (especially if you order it Swedish-style), another item brings plenty of meaty flavor to the table, along with a spicy element, too. Have you guessed it? It's the Sausage Burrito.

The Sausage Burrito features a soft tortilla, which encloses little nubs of pork sausage, pillowy scrambled eggs, melted cheese, and a mixture of tomatoes, onions, and green chiles, the latter of which are mostly mild but give the breakfast item just a kiss of spice. The burrito — which sells for $1.79 (price varies by location) — also comes with your choice of mild picante sauce or a hotter version if you like more heat.

One Reddit user said they've given "fancier" breakfast burritos a shot before, but "McDonald's with the small, dinky little burritos are still the best." It's a sentiment that is echoed around the internet, with fans declaring that while they aren't much to look at, they nonetheless fill a little burrito-sized hole in their hearts.

Not to pit two delicious McDonald's breakfast options against each other, but there are a few reasons why you might opt for a Sausage Burrito over a McMuffin. The first is that, if wrapped properly, burritos are much easier to eat on the go, including in your car, thanks to the fact that everything is contained inside the tortilla (versus the McMuffin, in which everything is layered and could slip around and possibly out of the English muffin). "Just ate two [of the burritos] on a road trip, loved 'em," one Redditor enthused. If you love spice, another user joked that "the rule is half a packet of picante per bite."

Another reason you might order the Sausage Burrito from McDonald's is if you have a taste for something with a bit more depth than your average breakfast sandwich. There's a symphony of flavors involved in the burrito, and aside from the slight spice of the filling, there are actually quite a few elements that go into these little tubes. The aforementioned green chiles and onions add a mild kick and savory depth, while the tomatoes (a known umami powerhouse) help give the burrito its fresh and surprisingly complex flavor profile.

#9653. The Clothes That Make People Appear More Intelligent

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

Wearing more clothing makes you look more competent, a study finds.

Something as simple as taking off a sweater is enough to make you look less competent, the researchers found.

The finding applies to both men and women, said Dr Kurt Gray, the study’s first author:

“An important thing about our study is that, unlike much previous research, ours applies to both sexes.

It also calls into question the nature of objectification because people without clothes are not seen as mindless objects, but they are instead attributed a different kind of mind.”

The effect occurs because seeing more flesh encourages us to think about a person’s body, rather than their mind.

“We also show that this effect can happen even without the removal of clothes.

Simply focusing on someone’s attractiveness, in essence concentrating on their body rather than their mind, makes you see her or him as less of an agent [someone who acts and plans] more of an experiencer.”

Showing bare skin, though, does have some advantages, explained Dr Gray:

“A focus on the body, and the increased perception of sensitivity and emotion it elicits might be good for lovers in the bedroom.

Others appear to be less inclined to harm people with bare skin and more inclined to protect them.

In one experiment, for example, people viewing male subjects with their shirts off were less inclined to give those subjects uncomfortable electric shocks than when the men had their shirts on.”

“Even more than robbing someone of agency, the increased experience that may accompany body perceptions may lead those who are characterized in terms of their bodies to be seen as more reactive and emotional, traits that may also serve to work against career advancement.”

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Gray et al., 2011).
